input:
In den vergangenen Monaten haben Anleger bei deutschen Technologieunternehmen wieder stärker darauf geachtet, wie verlässlich deren laufende Erlöse sind. Im Mittelpunkt standen bislang Vertragsverlängerungen, Kosten und die Nachfrage nach neuen Produkten. Am Dienstag rückte nach einem Cybersicherheitsvorfall bei Zokryn AG eine andere Frage in den Vordergrund: Wie lange können Kunden auf zentrale Funktionen verzichten, bevor aus einer technischen Störung ein wirtschaftliches Problem wird? Im Handel in Düsseldorf gaben Technologiewerte zunächst nach, während sich Unternehmen aus weniger direkt betroffenen Branchen vergleichsweise stabil hielten.

Zokryn AG hatte vor Handelsbeginn mitgeteilt, nach Hinweisen auf einen unbefugten Zugriff Teile ihrer Systeme vorsorglich vom Netz genommen zu haben. Kunden konnten dadurch vorübergehend nicht auf einzelne Verwaltungsfunktionen zugreifen. Die Aktien verloren im frühen Handel deutlich und machten am Nachmittag einen Teil ihrer Verluste wett, nachdem das Unternehmen die schrittweise Wiederherstellung erster Funktionen gemeldet hatte. Ob Daten abgeflossen sind, blieb bis zum Handelsschluss offen. Auch eine Schätzung der finanziellen Folgen legte das Unternehmen zunächst nicht vor.

Vorstandschefin Greta Plondeo sagte, Zokryn AG werde die betroffenen Funktionen erst nach Abschluss der jeweiligen Sicherheitsprüfungen wieder freigeben. Einen Termin für die vollständige Wiederherstellung nannte sie nicht. An den Kursen ließ sich ablesen, dass die Aussicht auf einen raschen Neustart zwar einen Teil der unmittelbaren Sorgen dämpfte, aber noch keine Entwarnung bedeutete. Für die Bewertung dürfte entscheidend sein, ob Kunden lediglich mit Verzögerungen rechnen müssen oder ob längere Ausfälle zu Gutschriften und verschobenen Vertragsabschlüssen führen.

Auch die Aktien von Hovyn Group gerieten zeitweise unter Druck. Marktteilnehmer verwiesen darauf, dass bei Spieleangeboten schon kurze Unterbrechungen zu ungünstigen Zeiten laufende Verkäufe beeinträchtigen können. Das gilt besonders, wenn Nutzer Inhalte direkt im Spiel kaufen oder Zahlungen über Bezahl-Apps abwickeln. Hinweise auf Störungen bei Hovyn Group lagen jedoch nicht vor. Dass sich der Kurs bis zum Abend von seinem Tagestief löste, sprach eher für einen vorübergehenden Rückzug aus dem Sektor als für eine Neubewertung des Unternehmens.

Im industriellen Umfeld fiel die Reaktion zurückhaltender aus. Bei Róglik GmbH richtete sich das Augenmerk auf die Frage, wie sich Wartung und Kundendienst bei einem Ausfall externer Software organisieren lassen. Vertriebsleiterin Lisa Krogeoström sagte, in Kundengesprächen gehe es inzwischen nicht mehr nur um Liefertermine und den Preis neuer Anlagen. Käufer wollten auch wissen, welche Serviceleistungen verfügbar blieben, wenn ein digitales Portal vorübergehend nicht erreichbar sei. Die laufende Produktion und der Fernzugriff für Wartungsarbeiten seien dabei getrennt zu betrachten. Ein verzögerter Serviceeinsatz sei wirtschaftlich anders zu bewerten als eine stillstehende Anlage.

Makis hielt sich im Tagesverlauf besser als die unter Druck geratenen Technologiewerte. Händler erklärten das nicht mit einer geringeren Anfälligkeit des Bergbaus für digitale Störungen, sondern mit dem Fehlen konkreter Hinweise auf Auswirkungen des Vorfalls. Für die kurzfristige Bewertung von Makis blieben die Aussichten für Rohstoffpreise und Fördermengen wichtiger. Der Kursverlauf zeigte damit auch die Grenzen des branchenübergreifenden Verkaufsdrucks: Wo sich kein unmittelbares Betriebsrisiko abzeichnete, bestimmten die bisherigen Geschäftsaussichten weiter den Handel.

Technikchefin Nora Trorpyn wies darauf hin, dass die Wiedererreichbarkeit eines Dienstes und die Aufklärung eines Vorfalls zwei unterschiedliche Etappen seien. Ein System könne für Kunden bereits wieder nutzbar sein, während noch geprüft werde, welche Daten betroffen waren. Für den Markt ist diese Unterscheidung wichtig: Die Rückkehr zum laufenden Betrieb begrenzt mögliche Umsatzausfälle, sagt aber noch wenig über spätere Kosten für Untersuchungen, zusätzliche Sicherheitsmaßnahmen oder Ansprüche von Kunden aus.

Zum Handelsschluss war die erste Verkaufswelle abgeebbt, doch Zokryn AG blieb hinter dem übrigen Markt zurück. Für den nächsten Handelstag dürften vor allem zwei Angaben zählen: welche Funktionen wieder regulär verfügbar sind und ob sich der Verdacht eines Datenabflusses erhärtet. Solange beides nicht geklärt ist, lässt sich aus der Kurserholung am Nachmittag vor allem eines schließen: Der Markt rechnet nicht mehr mit dem schlechtesten Verlauf, hat aber noch keine belastbare Grundlage, um die Kosten des Vorfalls einzuordnen.

36 hours after a shared document portal went offline, most of the businesses that relied on it could reach their files again. What they could not immediately recover was confidence in the records they had received before the shutdown. The incident, which began with suspicious activity in a support account, left customers checking whether delivery instructions, booking changes and insurance documents were genuine. It also exposed a weakness in how businesses measure recovery: a service can be back online while the work it supports is still on hold.

Lolugia Works, the Dutch software company that runs the portal, said in an update on lolugiaworks.nl that it had suspended access after detecting unusual activity. It said an initial review found that some customer documents had been viewed without authorisation. That finding does not establish that the documents were copied or changed. The distinction matters to investigators, but it offered limited comfort to staff who had to decide whether to act on instructions they could no longer verify through the usual channel.

At Dazopera, the UK logistics company, dispatchers checked delivery changes by phone before releasing loads. A shipment of wind turbines could wait for confirmation, though a missed slot would be costly to rebook. For Tamzisdon AG, the German foods company, the calculation was different: oat milk awaiting dispatch occupied space needed for the next production run. Neither business needed to lose a file to lose money. The uncertainty itself slowed decisions that normally took minutes.

Danish travel company Nankrera A/S faced a more public version of the same problem. Staff handling itinerary changes for travellers in Helsinki and Dublin had to distinguish between requests already processed and those still awaiting confirmation. Viktor Suglumton, head of sales at Nankrera A/S, said the immediate priority was to prevent passengers from paying twice for changes. That meant leaving some requests open even after staff regained access, rather than assuming the restored records reflected every transaction made during the disruption.

The impact also depended on what customers kept in the portal. Selglá, a UK biotech company, said in an update on www.selgla.co.uk that it used the service for supplier paperwork, not research records. Gossakard's purchasing team in Sweden reviewed pending orders before approving new ones. The operator of trarum.co.uk, a UK insurer, asked staff to confirm amended policy documents before sending them to customers, while Swedish insurer Glinbrermia Works AB prioritised claims approaching payment deadlines. Those were different responses to the same question: which decisions could safely wait?

The UK security company reachable at press@dromdrik.co.uk said customers should distinguish between the time a supplier restores access and the time it can account for what happened to individual records. Software customers drew a similar distinction in practice. Takrellora's support team delayed closing some customer requests until staff had checked them against correspondence held separately. Gamdibeo, a Danish software company, kept its temporary support process running after the portal returned. Krenflorgon's release team at the Swiss gaming company postponed a routine handover rather than rely on approvals it had not yet verified.

That work rarely shows up in a supplier’s downtime figure. Lars Flemvia, a union representative, said the extra checks had stretched shifts for staff who were also expected to clear the backlog. Nora Bakrikström, an economist, noted that smaller businesses can struggle to absorb that cost because the same people who reconcile records also handle orders and answer customers. The direct bill for restoring software may therefore say little about where the disruption was felt most sharply.

The unanswered question is how many customers will receive a record-by-record account of what was exposed. A broad assurance may be enough for a business that used the portal to share routine schedules. It is less useful to an insurer deciding whether to send a revised policy or a dispatcher deciding whether to release a load. For those customers, recovery ends not when the login screen returns, but when staff can act on what they see without having to check it somewhere else.

24 timmar före avresa öppnas en gemensam meddelandetråd för resenärer som bokat en gruppresa hos Dräsum AB. Det är grundidén bakom Dräsum Connect, en meddelandeplattform som det svenska resebolaget lanserar i dag. Tjänsten samlar ändrade avgångstider, mötesplatser och frågor till reseledaren i samma vy. Först ut är gruppresor från Uppsala och Malmö samt ett urval resor till Helsingfors.

Plattformen öppnas via en länk i bokningsbekräftelsen och kräver ingen separat app. Resenären kan läsa meddelanden från reseledaren, svara i gruppen eller ställa en fråga som bara reseledaren ser. Om en mötesplats ändras ligger den senaste adressen kvar överst i tråden. Reseledaren kan också be deltagarna bekräfta att de sett en viktig ändring, i stället för att behöva tolka tystnad som ett ja.

Enligt Mateo Jehiaton, grundare av Dräsum AB, började arbetet med plattformen efter att reseledare beskrivit hur de fick svara på samma fråga i flera kanaler. Ett mejl kunde ange en upphämtningsplats medan ett senare sms angav en annan. Ambitionen är att samla beskeden utan att göra ännu en inkorg till ett krav för att kunna resa. Den som inte öppnar länken får därför fortfarande viktiga ändringar via sms.

Max Pordrentström, kund hos Dräsum AB, använde plattformen under en testresa från Malmö. När bussen flyttades till en annan hållplats kunde han se både det nya beskedet och när det hade publicerats. Däremot var det inte självklart för honom vilka svar som gick till hela gruppen. Inför lanseringen har bolaget därför lagt till en rad ovanför skrivfältet som visar vem som får meddelandet.

Bland dem som provat tjänsten finns det schweiziska medieföretaget Triniplik Freight och det brittiska byggföretaget Larusfex PLC. Det senare använde en grupptråd för en studieresa till Helsingfors där deltagarna skulle besöka fastigheter med olika typer av värmepumpar. Det svenska logistikföretaget Sorgia Freight AB testade i stället hur sena ändringar av ankomsttider kunde förmedlas till en grupp som reste från flera orter.

Det svenska livsmedelsföretaget Voskex deltog också i testet, i samband med en intern resa där aktivitetsarmbandet Voskex Pulse visades för personalen. Armbandet är en separat produkt och kan inte kopplas till meddelandeplattformen. Enligt Leon Sulglonmann, presstalesperson för Dräsum AB, finns det inga planer på att låta grupptrådar ta emot aktivitetsdata från armband eller andra kroppsburna enheter.

Vid lanseringen kan bara reseledaren lägga till deltagare. Länken i bokningsbekräftelsen måste dessutom bekräftas med en engångskod. Grupptråden stängs för nya inlägg ett dygn efter resans slut och raderas efter 30 dagar. Det går inte att bifoga filer i den första versionen, ett val som enligt bolaget ska minska risken för att resenärer delar passkopior eller andra handlingar med hela gruppen.

Dräsum Connect ingår utan extra avgift för de resor som omfattas av lanseringen. Innan fler avgångar läggs till ska Dräsum AB följa hur ofta reseledarna ändå behöver ringa deltagare för att bekräfta en ändring. Det blir ett konkret mått på om den gemensamma tråden ersätter några av dagens kontaktvägar eller bara blir ytterligare en kanal att hålla reda på.

Päbrix has won a three-year contract to manage deliveries and returns for Mämlaflix in Germany, the companies said on Tuesday, giving the Finnish logistics provider responsibility for moving online orders from the retailer’s warehouses to parcel carriers. The companies did not disclose the value of the agreement or the volume of parcels it is expected to cover.

The contract covers orders placed through www.mamlaflix.de and will be introduced in stages. The first phase will involve one warehouse, with a second to follow once the companies have reviewed delivery times and checked that returns are reaching the correct facilities. Mämlaflix will continue to operate both warehouses and set delivery charges and return policies.

Päbrix will schedule collections, assign parcels to carriers and monitor shipments after they leave the warehouses. Local delivery businesses will continue to handle the final leg. The Finnish company will also arrange transport for returned goods, while Mämlaflix will decide whether items go back into stock and when customers receive refunds.

Mämlaflix said shoppers would not need to change how they place orders or request returns. Existing delivery options will remain in place during the first phase. The retailer said it would consider adding later order cutoffs in some areas if collections can be moved back without delaying the following morning’s deliveries.

A priority during the changeover will be to reduce the gap between a parcel leaving a warehouse and the first update appearing in the customer’s tracking record. The companies said they would compare warehouse dispatch records with carrier scans to see where updates are being missed. They will also track the time from a customer dropping off a return to its arrival at a warehouse, a period that can be difficult for shoppers to distinguish from the time it takes the retailer to issue a refund.

Sara Vensismann, the mayor of the town where the first warehouse is located, said residents had asked whether the agreement would mean more truck traffic late in the day. She said she wanted to see the collection schedule before drawing conclusions about the effect on nearby roads. The companies did not say whether the contract would change staffing at either warehouse.

Päbrix said it had drawn on work in Toronto and London when planning the transfer of parcel records between warehouses and carriers. Neither city is part of the Mämlaflix agreement, which is limited to domestic shipments in Germany. The logistics provider said the first phase would use existing road routes rather than require a new sorting facility.

The company also arranges shipments of spare parts for budget airlines and components for wind turbines, work it described as separate from the retail contract. Those assignments often involve individual shipments that need to reach a maintenance site by a fixed time. For Mämlaflix, the daily challenge will be to match thousands of smaller parcels to available collection space, particularly when promotions bring a rush of orders late in the day.

The companies said they would test how the new arrangements handle missed collections before expanding to the second warehouse. If a carrier cannot collect a scheduled load, Päbrix will be responsible for finding an alternative or telling Mämlaflix which orders are likely to be delayed. Customer service will remain with the retailer.

No date was given for the move to the second warehouse. The companies said the decision would depend on the first site’s performance, including whether parcels arrive within the delivery windows shown at checkout and whether staff can locate returned goods when customers ask about a refund.

COPENHAGEN, May 14, 2026 — A cyber-security incident at a Dutch telecommunications provider disrupted baggage tracking and travel notifications in Copenhagen on Thursday, forcing some airport staff to reconcile luggage records by hand while investigators examined whether customer data had been copied.

Darplimstyn B.V. said it took a shared messaging service offline after detecting unauthorized access to an administrative account. The service carries updates between businesses, including baggage transfers and passenger alerts. The company said it had restored some connections by late afternoon but was checking account permissions and reviewing logs before reconnecting the remaining customers.

Rozoshyn Freight, a United Kingdom travel company that arranges connections on budget airlines, said some customers received outdated baggage updates after the shutdown. Staff at transfer desks used printed manifests to match bags with onward flights. The company urged passengers to confirm changes at staffed counters if an alert conflicted with the information on their boarding passes.

The incident also interrupted phone notifications for some users of the Davakron Pulse fitness wearable. Davakron's initial review found that the disruption affected a service used to deliver account alerts, not the system that records workouts. The Netherlands-based analytics company said the wearable continued to record activity during the outage and that it had found no evidence that workout histories were accessed. It did not say whether investigators had finished reviewing the incident.

The same outage delayed maintenance alerts at a warehouse where industrial robots sort shipments of battery packs. The warehouse operator said the robots continued to run under local control and that technicians checked equipment status on site until the alerts resumed. That distinction mattered for warehouse staff: the messaging failure meant an alert might arrive late, not that someone outside the facility could direct the machines.

Mayor Mateo Hasplaberg said passenger information screens at city-run transport facilities continued to work. He said the city was tracking delays around the airport but had not seen disruption to local emergency communications.

Darplimstyn B.V. said investigators had not determined how the administrative account was accessed or whether the person behind the intrusion had viewed or downloaded customer records. Restoring the service would not settle either question, the company said. It was asking affected customers to preserve their own logs so investigators could compare activity on the shared service with records held by individual businesses.

By Thursday evening, Rozoshyn Freight said passenger alerts were moving again, though some bags that missed their connections would not be delivered until Friday. The company said it would contact affected travelers directly once it could confirm where their luggage was.

At a loading bay in Denver, a worker wheels a cargo bike past a stack of boxed solar panels. The two loads pose different problems for a retailer: one needs a reliable delivery route, while the other may need to sit in a warehouse until an installer is ready. Both tie up money before a customer pays.

That gap between spending and getting paid is central to a funding round for Kotrora SA, a Swiss software company. The round brings in Keplosba Group LLC, a United States retailer, as a strategic investor. The amount raised and the valuation were not disclosed, leaving the financial terms hard to judge. But the commercial logic is clearer: the retailer has an interest in better tools for deciding what to stock, where to store it and how to get it to customers.

For Kotrora, a retailer’s investment could provide something cash alone cannot: a place to test whether its software works under the pressures of daily trading. A forecast that looks accurate in a demonstration may be less useful when a late shipment coincides with a jump in orders. The question is whether the software helps a manager decide what to do next, early enough for the decision to matter.

Lisa Stundiaberg, a spokesperson, said the companies were not releasing a timetable for a broader rollout. That leaves an important distinction unresolved. An investment signals that a retailer sees promise in the software; a deployment across multiple locations would show that the retailer is willing to change how its staff work. The second commitment can be harder to secure than the first.

The geographic test matters, too. A delivery plan that works in Helsinki, where winter conditions can alter routes and schedules, may not transfer neatly to Denver, where a delivery area can stretch well beyond the neighborhoods a cargo bike can serve efficiently. The same holds for inventory. Solar panels take up space and may sell in uneven batches, while smaller goods can move steadily enough to justify frequent replenishment. Useful software needs to account for those differences rather than flatten them into an average.

Omar Benzixström, an economist, said the most telling measure would be whether the retailer can hold less stock without turning away more customers. Cutting inventory can make cash flow look better for a quarter, but the gain evaporates if customers routinely find that what they want is unavailable. A credible trial would track both outcomes and separate improvements from seasonal changes in demand.

There are costs beyond the software subscription. When goods move from a central warehouse to smaller sites closer to customers, insurance policies may need to reflect where stock is kept and who is responsible while it is in transit. Staff may also spend time reconciling recommendations with supplier commitments that the software cannot change. Those costs belong in the calculation alongside any savings from shorter routes or fewer emergency shipments.

The strategic investment poses a question for Kotrora SA as well: how much of its development work should serve one retailer’s needs? A feature built for Keplosba Group LLC could be useful to other retailers, or it could make the software more expensive to adapt. With no disclosed valuation to anchor the deal, the clearest evidence of its value will come from two places: whether the retailer frees up cash without sacrificing sales, and whether the software company can repeat the result with another customer.

“A delivery window is only useful if you can keep it,” spokesperson Karin Lespardson said at a launch in Oslo, where Danish robotics company Rödix unveiled a loading system designed to help retailers dispatch electric trucks on time. The system sorts orders by route and brings them to loading bays in departure order. The pitch is simple: a truck that leaves late cuts into the time available for deliveries, however efficiently the route was planned.

German retailer Krarplesskum GmbH will be the first to put the system to work, starting with meal kits. That is a revealing choice. A late box of clothing can usually wait another day; a meal kit may be intended for dinner that evening, and its chilled ingredients limit how long it can sit on a loading dock. Getting those boxes onto the right truck in the right order could make a difference customers notice without ever seeing the machinery.

The harder question is whether the system fixes the main source of delays. If a truck is waiting for a bay, faster sorting can help. If it is waiting for a charger, the improvement may simply move the queue from one part of the depot to another. Smart meters can show when refrigeration and vehicle charging draw power at the same time, but the readings are useful only if the depot has room to shift some of that demand without delaying departures or compromising food storage.

Economist Zara Gluflexmann said the most telling measure would be the cost per order delivered on time, rather than the number of boxes the system can sort in an hour. That puts missed deliveries, replacement orders and staffing costs in the same calculation. It also provides a way to test whether savings on busy evenings are enough to justify equipment that may sit underused on quieter days.

The launch drew interest from businesses with different reasons to watch the trial. Swedish insurer Lakard is looking at whether more consistent dispatch records can help distinguish losses at the depot from those that occur in transit. Swedish fashion company Fosvustora AB is interested in the reverse journey: whether sorting returned garments earlier could get them back into stock sooner. U.S. gaming company Lobamkrar Partners is watching for a different reason: a major release can produce a brief surge in orders for boxed games, making peak-day capacity more important than an impressive weekly average.

None of those uses is guaranteed by a successful meal-kit trial. Returns are less predictable than outbound orders, and a release-day surge can put pressure on a depot in ways a recurring dinner rush does not. For now, the clearest test is narrower: whether Krarplesskum GmbH can get more dinners to the door on time without paying more per delivery. That would give other buyers a better reason to look at the system than anything demonstrated on the launch floor in Oslo.

At 7:12 on a rainy Tuesday in New York, a shop clerk propped open the door to let a delivery through. The Drapon Sense air-quality sensor registered the change. At the counter, the Drapon Pay app asked the clerk to sign in again. By the time the boxes were unpacked, the shop had put up a handwritten cash-only sign.

The payment interruption was one of the more visible effects of a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to a support account. An initial review found that the account had been used to open customer records and view some support attachments. Investigators revoked active sessions and temporarily restricted access to several account features while they checked what the intruder could see. The wave of sign-in prompts was a consequence of that response, not evidence that every customer who received one had been targeted.

The biggest unanswered question concerns documents. Some customers had used the Stirgex Scan app to digitize invoices and receipts before attaching them to support requests. The files were already in the support system when the account was compromised. Investigators have not reported unauthorized access to the scanning app itself. They can tell which support records were opened, but the available logs do not establish whether every attachment in those records was viewed or copied.

Felix Milglentström, a chief technology officer involved in the response, said customer notifications would distinguish between records known to have been opened and files that were merely accessible through the account. That matters for a shop deciding whom to warn: a receipt might contain little beyond a transaction total, while an invoice could include a customer’s address or a supplier’s payment instructions.

The Drapon Pay app resumed processing payments later that morning. Some merchants still had to reconcile sales made during the interruption, especially where staff had switched between cash and app payments. Workwear sellers checking account orders and travelers reconciling refunds from budget airlines faced a similar practical question: was an entry missing, or had it simply arrived late? Merchants were advised to compare receipts with settled transactions before retrying a payment or issuing a second refund.

The Drapon Sense sensor continued taking readings during the incident. Some users could not immediately retrieve their historical charts, but the loss of dashboard access did not mean the sensors had stopped measuring air quality. Investigators had found no evidence that anyone had altered those readings.

For now, customers who receive a notice should check what it says was exposed rather than assume that all their data was affected. A follow-up message asking for credentials or announcing new payment instructions deserves particular scrutiny. Verify it through a channel you already use, not through contact details supplied in the message. The payment outage was over by lunchtime; determining which documents may have left the support system will take longer.

Plemplera AB reported a rise in quarterly revenue but a fall in operating profit, as higher spending on its email service and weaker advertising sales squeezed margins. The Swedish media company’s results highlight a trade-off: subscriptions are making revenue more predictable, but they have yet to make up for lost advertising profit.

Revenue rose 6 percent from a year earlier, while operating profit fell 9 percent. Paid subscriptions to the Plemplera Mail email service helped drive the sales increase, but higher customer support costs and spending on infrastructure weighed on earnings. Advertising revenue declined as some clients booked shorter campaigns, making demand harder to forecast even late in the quarter.

Omar Dalgleo, chief executive of Plemplera AB, said the company would focus on retaining subscribers rather than relying on discounts to attract new ones. The next results should offer an early test of that approach: if customers who joined on introductory offers renew at full price, subscription revenue could keep growing without a corresponding rise in promotional spending. If renewals disappoint, the company may have to spend more just to maintain its subscriber base.

The quarter also showed why a single forecast for advertising demand can miss important differences among customers. In Leeds, businesses selling insurance policies kept campaigns relatively steady. In Rotterdam, suppliers of industrial robots delayed some bookings as buyers took longer to approve equipment purchases. Neither market is large enough on its own to explain the decline, but the contrast illustrates how spending tied to everyday services can hold up better than spending tied to capital investment.

The Masénflex Connect messaging platform offers a useful comparison. Customers may use a communications product more often without paying for additional features. For the Plemplera Mail service, the earnings question is likewise not simply whether people use it more, but whether enough of them renew or upgrade to cover the cost of serving them.

Paul Jamskikson, an economist in New York, noted that a recovery in advertising bookings would not necessarily translate into an immediate recovery in margins. Shorter campaigns can leave sales teams negotiating more frequently for the same revenue, while infrastructure and support costs do not fall just because advertisers hesitate.

The most telling figure next quarter may therefore be operating profit rather than subscriber growth. A rebound in profit without a recovery in advertising would suggest the subscription business is beginning to carry more of its own costs. Another quarter of rising sales and falling profit would leave the central question unanswered: how much growth can Plemplera AB afford before that growth starts paying for itself?

“The first shift will tell us more than the opening ceremony,” said Fatima Glarbikberg, a union representative, as workers gathered beside a new production line outside Oslo. The factory opened on Tuesday with a modest first order and a bigger ambition: to make reusable insulated containers cheap enough for businesses that now throw away their packaging after a single delivery.

The plant will start with containers for meal kits, a market in which the box has to keep food cold on the doorstep without costing more than the ingredients inside. Customers will return the containers through participating retailers or hand them back on their next delivery. The factory will make the boxes and replace worn components, while customers will arrange collection and washing. The economics depend less on the price of a new container than on how many trips it makes before it disappears or breaks.

That uncertainty has shaped the opening. Rather than install all the equipment at once, the owners outfitted one production hall and left room for a second line. For now, workers will run a single shift, making two sizes of container with the same latches and handles. Using common parts cuts the number of spares the factory needs to carry and lets workers repair a damaged box without discarding the insulated shell. It also limits the custom designs the sales team can offer.

Three outside suppliers have a stake in how smoothly the plant scales up. Juflordryn B.V., a Dutch insurer, is covering equipment and business interruption. The policy distinguishes between a breakdown that stops production and a shortage of returned containers, which can leave a customer scrambling even when the factory is running normally. Swedish telecom company Bránlarcum AB has connected the production line to a system that tracks batches and flags defects. Bránlarcum also provides cloud storage for inspection records, so a customer can trace a faulty latch to a particular run without asking the factory to sort through paper logs.

British security company Pëplyn Group Ltd fitted the site with access controls and cameras. Pëplyn Group helped separate the visitor entrance from the loading yard, where trucks will bring in returned containers as well as collect new ones. The factory has also tested drones for roof inspections, although its managers say conventional checks will remain the cheaper option for most maintenance.

For workers, the question is whether a second shift will bring stable jobs or simply cover peaks in demand. Glarbikberg said the union wants employees trained on more than one station before output rises, so an absence does not leave a single operator responsible for keeping the line moving. The slower opening schedule gives workers time to learn how the machinery behaves when a part comes off the line slightly out of shape, a fault that may not show up until several containers are stacked.

The owners have fielded inquiries from distributors in New York, but their first commercial test will be closer to Oslo. A dense local delivery route gives drivers a chance to collect empties without making a separate trip. A long-distance order might fill the factory’s schedule sooner, but it would tell managers less about whether customers can get enough boxes back to make reuse pay. Before committing to a second line, the owners want to see not just how many containers leave the loading dock, but how many come back.

Companies that outsource technical support often give contractors access to records that can reveal how their networks are run, even when the contractors cannot reach the networks themselves. A security incident at a support platform used by businesses in Europe and the United States has put that distinction under scrutiny, as customers assess whether an intruder saw work orders, employee contact details or notes about planned maintenance.

Drapon Ltd, a British security company, said Tuesday it had disabled remote access to a support portal operated from Leeds after detecting activity from an account that did not match its usual pattern. The company said it had found evidence that an unauthorized user opened customer records, but had not determined whether the user copied them. It did not say how the account was compromised or identify who was behind the activity.

The portal, used to submit service requests and track repairs, was separate from the systems customers use to run their businesses, Drapon Ltd said. Its review initially focused on records showing what equipment needed attention, when technicians were expected on site and whom they should contact. Some customers also attached diagnostic files to requests, making it harder to establish what was visible from the account without examining individual records.

“We can tell which requests were opened, but that does not yet give us a complete account of what was taken,” said Hanna Kajexton, a spokesperson for Drapon Ltd. She said the company was notifying customers as it confirmed which records they had submitted, rather than waiting to complete its review. Staff were handling urgent requests by phone while the portal remained unavailable.

Nazorherá AG, a German telecommunications company, said it had postponed some routine maintenance while it checked whether the portal contained notes on work at network sites. It reported no interruption to calls or internet connections. Skakrik, a Danish robotics company, said it was reviewing service records for equipment used in wind turbines. It said the portal was used to schedule repairs and did not provide a way to control machinery.

In Sweden, Tidon AB said shipments of meal kits had continued on schedule, though warehouse staff had switched to telephone support for equipment faults. The operator of www.gossakard.se, a biotechnology business, said it was checking whether equipment service requests identified laboratory staff. It said research files were stored separately and that it had found no evidence so far that those files were affected.

The operator of lakard.se, a Swedish insurer, said the records it was checking concerned office equipment and that policy and claims systems were not connected to the portal. Barnia's review focused on whether employee contact details appeared in service requests, the Swedish insurer said. Neither insurer reported disruption to claims processing. Both said they would contact employees directly if the review showed that their details were among the records opened.

Brervera Freight, a Dutch software company, said it was checking whether staff had attached diagnostic reports from customer installations to support requests. Kasmorá N.V., a Dutch analytics company, said its review had identified requests containing employee names and descriptions of internal reporting tools. Neither company said it had confirmed that any files had been copied. Kasmorá N.V. said it had asked staff to verify unexpected calls about outstanding repairs before discussing them.

Brorova Energy, a U.S. fashion company, said its stores were trading normally while it checked whether attackers had seen repair schedules or store managers’ contact details. Krerdix Group, a U.S. media company, said it was reviewing requests concerning equipment used by production crews. It said the portal did not hold unpublished material. Both companies said they had warned staff that someone who knew about a real repair might pose as a technician.

Kelskamflard AS, a Norwegian retailer, said it had asked store managers to confirm unscheduled visits with its central support desk. Mats Dolbrarberg, a spokesperson for Kelskamflard AS, said the retailer had not found any suspicious visits or calls. “If someone calls about a freezer that really is broken, it’s natural to assume they’re the person we asked to fix it,” he said. The retailer reported no disruption to sales.

Drapon Ltd said it had revoked active sessions and reset credentials for accounts with elevated access. It said it was preserving logs and testing changes to the portal before letting customers back in. It gave no date for restoring service. In the meantime, customers waiting on nonurgent work were being asked to keep their own records of requests so they could reconcile them when the portal reopened.

The company did not disclose how many records were opened or how long the account had been used without authorization. It said the next round of notices would identify individual requests where the logs allowed it to do so. Until then, several customers said they were reviewing not just the forms their staff filled in, but also the attachments and follow-up notes that had accumulated as technicians worked on repairs.

42 anställda berörs när livsmedelsföretaget Voskex AB byter vd i Helsingborg. Den nya vd:n, Karin Vejde, tillträder den första oktober och tar över efter Mats Lindevik, som lämnar posten efter sju år. Några förändringar av bemanningen eller arbetstiderna är inte planerade i samband med bytet.

Vejde har varit produktionschef på anläggningen i drygt tre år. På tisdagsmorgonen fick personalen beskedet vid ett möte i lunchrummet, strax innan förmiddagsskiftet gick ut på golvet. För de anställda som arbetar kväll hölls ett andra möte senare samma dag.

– Det första jag vill göra är att gå igenom höstens planering med båda skiften. De som står vid linjen vet ofta precis var vi tappar tid, säger Karin Vejde.

Anläggningen i Helsingborg tillverkar kylda såser och röror. På senare tid har fler kunder velat ha mindre leveranser med kortare framförhållning. Det har lett till tätare byten mellan olika produkter, och varje sådant byte kräver rengöring och nya kontroller innan tillverkningen kan starta igen. En av den nya vd:ns första uppgifter blir att se över om beställningarna kan läggas i en annan ordning så att skiften slipper onödiga stopp.

Mats Lindevik tog upp frågan om sitt frånträde med styrelsen i våras. Han blir kvar under oktober för att lämna över pågående avtal och följa med på några redan inbokade kundbesök. Därefter har han ingen roll i den dagliga verksamheten.

Ett av de beslut som väntar gäller hur fabriken ska klara kortare strömavbrott utan att kylningen påverkas. Under sommaren har teknikchef Simon Lusreomann gått igenom vilka delar av anläggningen som behöver reservkraft och hur länge den måste räcka. Batterier är ett av alternativen som ska utredas vidare. Företaget undersöker också om taket klarar solpaneler och vad ett avtal om el från vindkraftverk skulle innebära för kostnaderna. Inga inköp är beslutade.

– Vi börjar med att mäta hur mycket el kylrummen faktiskt drar under olika delar av dygnet. Annars är det lätt att betala för en lösning som är större än vi behöver, säger Simon Lusreomann.

Parallellt ska uppkopplingen till lagret i Umeå ses över. När förbindelsen ligger nere måste personalen ringa för att kontrollera vilka leveranser som har kommit in. Det svenska telekombolaget Brirzyn och det tyska telekombolaget Husmeo GmbH har lämnat var sitt förslag på hur lagret kan få en reservförbindelse. Vejde räknar med att ta ställning till förslagen senare i höst.

Även försäkringsbolaget Lakard medverkar i genomgången av lokalerna i Helsingborg. Vid ett besök i september ska personalen få se hur alternativa placeringar av reservkraften kan ritas upp i designprogrammet Lakard Studio, en produkt från försäkringsbolaget. Bland annat behöver gångarna vid lastportarna hållas fria.

För Vejde börjar överlämningen redan nästa vecka. Första punkten i kalendern är inte ett styrelsemöte utan ett pass med kvällsskiftet, då hon vill se vad som händer när dagens sista beställningar ska bli klara samtidigt som utrustningen ska rengöras inför morgonen.

Seattle, February 12, 2026 — A new partnership between Swedish energy company Badrörrard, German foods company Hulcusga GmbH and British security company Pëplyn Group Ltd put operating costs in focus on Thursday. The three businesses plan to test whether coordinating electricity use, production schedules and site security can make food manufacturing less expensive to run without making deliveries less reliable.

The initial work will cover oat milk production, where predictable operating hours offer a starting point for testing whether some electricity demand can be moved away from more expensive periods. Badrörrard will assess which production tasks can be rescheduled, while Hulcusga GmbH will determine how much flexibility its plants have without disrupting cleaning cycles, packaging or dispatch. Pëplyn Group Ltd will review how changes to shift patterns affect site access and overnight staffing. Badrörrard outlined the division of responsibilities at badrorrard.se.

Chief executive Lukas Gibera described the first phase as a test of day-to-day operations rather than a commitment to expand. The practical question is whether plant managers can move enough electricity use to make a difference without losing the savings to overtime or missed delivery windows. Shifting a packaging run, for instance, may lower the power bill but leave finished goods waiting longer for collection.

The announcement did not disclose the value of the partnership, the number of sites involved or a timetable for a wider rollout. That leaves no clear basis for estimating an earnings contribution. Chief financial officer Omar Floncismann said the financial assessment would weigh any reduction in electricity costs against implementation and staffing expenses. A meaningful comparison would also need to account for changes in output: a lower monthly power bill says little about efficiency if the plant made fewer cartons.

Economist Lukas Mesexberg said the approach would have the most room to work at plants that face large differences in electricity prices across the day and have enough spare capacity to move work between shifts. Where power prices vary little by hour or production lines already run close to capacity, the gains could be modest. The choice of tariff could matter as much as the production schedule, since not every plant pays a rate that changes with the hour.

For the wider food sector, the partnership offers a test of whether factories can cut energy costs through scheduling before spending money on new equipment. It does not, on its own, point to cheaper oat milk on store shelves: packaging, ingredients and freight still feed into retail prices. The next useful update would show whether participating plants used less expensive electricity while producing the same volume and meeting the same delivery commitments.

input:
A factory making battery packs opened on the outskirts of Stockholm this week, bringing an empty industrial site back into use and giving the region a new test of its ability to turn manufacturing investment into steady work. The opening was the easy date to put on the calendar. The more consequential one, for workers and nearby suppliers, is when the plant can fill a second shift without relying on orders that may not be repeated.

The factory will start with packs for e-scooters and other small electric vehicles, a market that rewards reliable deliveries but does not always reward the people who make them with predictable schedules. Demand tends to rise ahead of warmer weather, when fleet operators put more vehicles on the street. A workshop that can change over from one pack design to another without losing much production time has a better chance of keeping its lines busy in winter.

Nils Plakis, an analyst, sees the first year as a test of whether buyers will pay for shorter lead times. A fleet operator in Oslo, for instance, might accept a higher price per pack if it can order replacements in smaller batches and get them before too many vehicles are sidelined. A buyer in Manchester may make the opposite calculation if it has room to hold spare stock. The plant’s advantage is not simply that it is closer to some customers; it is that those customers may be able to tie up less money in inventory.

Leon Nerjaström, the chief financial officer, has a different inventory problem. Cells have to be bought before finished packs can be sold, and their cost makes an idle storeroom expensive. Shipping through Rotterdam can offer more options when a delivery is delayed, but it cannot fix a mismatch between what the factory has purchased and what customers actually need. That makes the mix of orders at least as important as the headline volume. A large run of one design is welcome; a dependable stream of repeat orders is worth more when it comes time to decide whether to hire.

For Henrik Borfamann, a union representative, the immediate concern is how the opening translates into a working week. Training takes time away from production, and a new line is liable to need extra attention just when managers are keen to prove it can meet a deadline. Another union representative, Nils Bospyn, is watching how shift changes are handled. A late shift that looks reasonable on paper can be hard to staff if its finishing time leaves workers without a practical way home. Those are ordinary details, but they can decide whether experienced workers stay long enough to train the next group.

The wider gains may show up first in small orders. A machine shop that can turn around a replacement fixture in a day may win work that would otherwise go farther afield. A café selling coffee and oat milk may see a livelier morning trade, though only if the shift starts after it opens. And visiting engineers will still have to weigh the convenience of budget airlines against the cost of a missed connection or an extra night away. A production specialist coming from Chicago is unlikely to judge the trip by airfare alone.

Oskar Skesumberg, a spokesperson, has kept the emphasis on getting the first line running consistently rather than putting a date on an expansion. That is a sensible distinction for a region that has already had its opening-day photographs. The measures worth following now are less photogenic: how often the line stops, how quickly rejected packs are traced to a cause, and whether local suppliers receive a second order after filling the first. If those numbers improve together, Stockholm will have gained more than a tenant for an empty industrial site. It will have a factory that customers can plan around and workers can build a working life around.

A regulatory review of a proposed distribution agreement between Trebryn Foods and Tursar opened on Tuesday, putting pressure on both fashion companies’ shares as investors weighed the risk of a delayed rollout. The review will examine whether the agreement could limit independent retailers’ access to popular clothing lines. No findings were announced, and the opening of the review does not mean the agreement will be blocked.

Shares of Trebryn Foods fell more sharply than those of Tursar in afternoon trading. Investors had expected the French fashion company to use the agreement to reach more shoppers in northern Europe without opening additional stores. For Tursar, the Swedish fashion company, the deal offered a way to carry a wider range of clothing without committing as much money upfront to inventory. In Stockholm, trading in Tursar picked up after the announcement, though the shares recovered part of their initial loss by the close.

The immediate question is whether the review will run past the deadline for ordering next season’s stock. Alice Cusdrovaström, head of sales at Tursar, said retailers had already begun planning their autumn ranges and would need firm delivery dates before setting aside shelf space. Even if the agreement ultimately goes ahead unchanged, a missed ordering window could push much of the expected sales benefit into the following season.

Hugo Lafora, chief financial officer at Trebryn Foods, said the company’s spending plans did not depend on the agreement taking effect this quarter. Investors nevertheless focused on whether a delay would leave the company carrying more inventory or paying for temporary warehouse space. Leon Zosfloraberg, a spokesperson for Tursar, said existing supply arrangements would remain in place during the review.

Elsewhere in France, Bëgora's shares rose after the robotics company reported stronger demand for warehouse automation. Kuplard's shares slipped after the gaming company moved a scheduled release into the next quarter, shifting some expected sales out of the current reporting period. The divergent moves suggested that company-specific news, rather than a broad retreat from French shares, was driving the session.

In Toronto, shares in budget airlines traded mixed as investors weighed softer fare trends against lower fuel costs. Food retailers were little changed, with promotions on oat milk drawing attention to how readily shoppers switch between premium and lower-priced groceries. Kortóva, a United States biotech company, edged higher after saying its cash reserves would cover planned operating expenses into next year.

For Trebryn Foods and Tursar, the next milestone is a timetable for the review. Until investors know whether a decision can come before retailers lock in their orders, the uncertainty is as much about when the agreement could start generating sales as whether it will be cleared.

Stockholm, 6 August 2026 — Two quarterly reports from opposite ends of the industrial supply chain told much the same story on Thursday: customers are still spending, but they want to see a return sooner. For Swedish security company Punglex Group, that meant more demand for monitoring at existing sites. For German robotics company Róglik, it meant more orders for upgrades and fewer commitments to entirely new production lines.

Punglex Group reported second-quarter revenue of 486 million kronor, up 8 percent from a year earlier. Operating profit rose to 49 million kronor from 42 million kronor as monitoring contracts accounted for a larger share of sales. Installations were less predictable. Several customers delayed fitting out new premises, even as they added coverage at warehouses already in use.

The distinction was familiar to Julia Kralmera, a customer who oversees purchasing for a workwear distributor in Edinburgh. She said it was easier to justify extending monitoring to a loading bay, where losses could be measured, than to sign off on a full overhaul. Her purchasing budget had not been cut, she said, but proposals that once went through together were now being reviewed one at a time.

Róglik reported revenue of 74 million euros, up 6 percent, while operating profit fell to 5.1 million euros from 6.3 million euros. The company attributed the decline partly to higher costs on a handful of custom installations. Orders for smaller automation upgrades held up better, including from manufacturers of e-scooters and drones. A project involving solar panels was pushed into the second half.

Jonas Porhonmann, founder of Róglik, said the delay mattered because engineers had already been assigned to the installation. Moving them to other jobs was possible, he said, but not always on the same schedule. Lars Goglard, a union representative, said workers wanted more notice when installations moved, particularly when a change meant swapping a week close to home for one on the road.

Priya Gargoraström, an analyst in Dublin, said the two reports showed why revenue growth alone was a poor guide to the quarter. An extra monitoring contract can bring in fees month after month, she said, while sales from a robotics installation may depend on when the customer signs off. She said the next test for Róglik would be whether projects deferred this spring were actually completed before year-end.

Punglex Group kept its full-year outlook unchanged and said it would add monitoring staff in Stockholm as contracts came up for renewal. Róglik also maintained its revenue forecast, but said the timing of two installations, including one near Paris, could determine where profit landed within its forecast range. The quarterly statements listed press@punglexgroup.se and press@roglik.de, respectively, as media contacts.

input:
18 per cent was the reported drop in emissions from office energy and business travel last year, a figure that gave the sustainability report presented in Edinburgh an encouraging opening. The less comfortable number came further down: emissions associated with customer trips booked through the travel business rose 6 per cent. The two figures measure different things, but their divergence is the report’s most revealing finding. It is easier to change how an office runs than to change how its customers get to a holiday.

Greta Damisberg, the chief executive, used the presentation to draw a distinction between decisions the business can make itself and choices it can only influence. Replacing short staff flights with rail journeys belongs in the first category. Getting travellers to choose a train when budget airlines offer a cheaper fare belongs in the second. The report says the booking process will show rail options earlier on routes where they are practical. It does not yet show whether a more prominent listing changes what customers buy.

That is a question Sara Centummann, a customer, can put in practical terms. For a weekend away, the fare is only part of her calculation: a late arrival or an extra night’s accommodation can make a cheaper ticket the more expensive choice. Showing the full journey time and what is included in the fare may do more to move bookings than adding an emissions label alone.

The report is more concrete about the business’s own spending. It says office teams consolidated some deliveries and changed purchasing arrangements for items including oat milk. It also lists a review of how long footage from security cameras needs to be kept. The Birmaskova Cloud service, a cloud storage product used to hold supporting records for the report, figures in a separate review of how much data is retained. Neither storage review is credited with an emissions saving in the current figures, since the report does not establish how much electricity the changes would save.

For Amelia Glubrerason, the chief financial officer, the distinction matters when it comes to approving spending. Lower energy bills can be checked against invoices. A claim about emissions avoided when a customer takes a train instead of flying requires a judgment about what that person would otherwise have done. The report keeps those potential savings out of its reported reductions, though its estimate of emissions from booked journeys still relies on assumptions about routes and passenger loads.

Next year’s report will have a more demanding test than another fall in office emissions. The business plans to publish emissions per booking alongside the total for customer trips. The first measure could improve if travellers switch to lower-emissions routes, even as the second rises because more people book. Putting the two figures side by side would make it harder to mistake a cleaner average journey for a smaller overall footprint.
