input:
Cemflia lanserade på tisdagen i Stockholm ett styrsystem som ska hjälpa butiker, lager och fabriker att flytta delar av sin elförbrukning till billigare timmar. Det svenska energibolaget riktar sig först till företag som redan har utrustning vars drift går att planera om utan att leveranser försenas eller arbetsmiljön försämras. Den första installationen ska göras i ett lager i Helsingborg, där Cemflia ska pröva om besparingen blir tillräckligt stor för att bära kostnaden för både installation och abonnemang.

Systemet samlar in mätvärden och gör ett schema för nästa dygn utifrån elpris, väderprognos och verksamhetens egna driftkrav. Värmepumpar kan till exempel värma upp en lokal något tidigare än vanligt om elen är billig före arbetsdagens början. I en fabrik kan vissa arbetsmoment för industrirobotar läggas om, förutsatt att ändringen inte skapar kö längre fram i produktionen. Även laddning av drönare som används vid lagerinventering kan flyttas. Däremot ska utrustning som behövs för en pågående leverans inte behöva vänta på ett lägre elpris.

Under visningen i Stockholm fick en simulerad eftermiddag illustrera hur det kan se ut. När flera maskiner enligt det ordinarie schemat skulle starta samtidigt föreslog systemet att två starter skulle senareläggas. När sluttiden för en leverans sedan flyttades fram försvann ett av förslagen. Enligt teknikchef Johan Tarora är det just de ändringarna som personalen behöver kunna följa: om ett schema ändras ska den som ansvarar för driften kunna se varför och återgå till den vanliga planen. Visningen gav däremot inget besked om hur stor besparingen blir i en verklig anläggning.

Det tyska logistikbolaget Nanera AG medverkar i försöket i Helsingborg. I lagret är tiden mellan den sista plockrundan och kvällens avgångar ofta knapp, vilket begränsar vilka arbetsmoment som kan flyttas. Försöket börjar därför med uppvärmning och laddning, där det finns mer utrymme att ändra tider utan att röra packningen. Förutom elkostnaden ska försöket följa hur ofta personalen behöver frångå schemat. Om det sker regelbundet kan administrationen äta upp en del av vinsten, även om elräkningen sjunker.

Det svenska detaljhandelsbolaget Vorora AB undersöker samtidigt om systemet kan användas i butiker där uppvärmning och ventilation står för en betydande del av elanvändningen. Där är frågan inte bara när utrustningen kan köras, utan också vem som har rätt att ändra inställningarna. I hyrda lokaler kan fastighetsägaren ansvara för värmen medan hyresgästen betalar delar av elkostnaden. En besparing som ser lönsam ut för lokalen som helhet behöver då inte vara det för den part som ska betala för installationen.

För det norska modebolaget Sinpyn ASA och det svenska modebolaget Lonholbra AB ligger intresset snarare i hur logistiken påverkas under veckor med många returer. Båda har deltagit i samtal inför lanseringen, men ingen av dem har aviserat något köp. När nya varor ska ut samtidigt som returer tas emot kan det vara svårare att skjuta upp laddning eller flytta arbetsmoment. Om systemet främst sparar pengar under lugna veckor blir kalkylen en annan än om det fungerar när lagret är som mest belastat.

Cemflia planerar att ta betalt för installationen och därefter för ett abonnemang. Något generellt pris presenterades inte i Stockholm. Kostnaden ska bland annat bero på vilka mätare som redan finns och hur mycket arbete som krävs för att ansluta utrustningen. För kunden spelar också elavtalet roll. Med timpris kan det löna sig att flytta förbrukningen även om antalet kilowattimmar är oförändrat. Om nätavgiften påverkas av hur mycket el som används samtidigt kan färre toppar ge en besparing av ett annat slag. De två effekterna behöver därför redovisas var för sig.

I Helsingborg blir den första uppgiften att fastställa vad lagret skulle ha förbrukat utan den nya styrningen. En kall vecka eller ett ovanligt stort varuflöde räcker för att göra en enkel jämförelse mellan två elräkningar missvisande. Först när kostnaden kan jämföras mellan dagar med liknande väder och arbetsbelastning går det att bedöma vad schemat faktiskt bidrar med. Det beskedet väger tyngre för en köpare än hur smidigt systemet flyttade två maskinstarter under visningen i Stockholm.

Just before dawn in Berlin, a technician watched a routine diagnostics report stall halfway through loading. On the workshop floor, the robots kept moving. It was the missing report, not a stopped machine, that first drew attention to a cybersecurity incident at Róglik GmbH.

The German robotics company said an intruder gained access to a support portal used to exchange diagnostic files with customers. Róglik took the portal offline after spotting unusual downloads and began reviewing which files had been opened. The company said it had found no evidence that the intruder reached production networks or issued commands to equipment. That distinction matters: the portal held information about machines, but it was not used to control them.

Lukas Jipon, a spokesperson for Róglik GmbH, said the company was contacting customers whose files appeared in the download records. Some of those files contained equipment serial numbers, maintenance notes and staff contact details. Jipon said investigators were still checking whether older reports contained more sensitive material. The company has not said how many customers were affected or how long the intruder had access before the downloads were detected.

The disruption was felt as far away as Denver, where a maintenance team had to postpone a remote review of equipment used to assemble e-scooters. The workshop continued operating, but technicians set aside a recurring fault they had planned to investigate with outside help. A separate customer that makes smart meters said it was checking the diagnostic files it had previously shared. Neither customer reported a disruption to devices already in use.

Two analytics companies are examining different parts of the incident. Boglora PLC, based in the United Kingdom, is reconstructing the sequence of downloads from the portal’s records. Plenkia AB, based in Sweden, is helping classify the files so customers can distinguish routine service data from material that warrants a closer look. Johan Zamnis, an analyst, cautioned that a download record can show that a file was retrieved, but not whether the person who retrieved it read or shared it. Incomplete records can also make it difficult to establish the full scope of an incident.

Sibera GmbH, another German robotics company, said it had reviewed its own customer support arrangements after hearing about the incident. It reported no related intrusion. Its review focused on a question that applies well beyond robotics: how much information needs to remain available in a support portal after a repair is finished?

For customers, the next useful update will be a file-by-file accounting, not simply a date for the portal to reopen. A serial number may require little follow-up on its own, while a maintenance report with staff details and a description of a production line may need more attention. Until Róglik completes that review, the incident’s clearest consequence is a loss of visibility into what left the portal, even as the machines kept running.

On a grey morning in Stockholm, workers arriving for the early shift passed a row of boxed heat pumps on their way to a staff meeting. By the time they returned to the floor, the founder was no longer running the business.

Fatima Skirhera, the founder, handed day-to-day control to chief technology officer Omar Jelex, a decision that puts an engineer in charge just as the manufacturer faces pressure to improve deliveries and after-sales service. The handover changes who makes those decisions. It does not, on its own, settle which parts of the business will get the money and staff they need.

Jonas Pasixström, a spokesperson, said the immediate priority was to keep existing orders moving. That may reassure buyers waiting for equipment, but it says little about how Jelex will manage a portfolio that stretches from security cameras to components for wind turbines. The products share some engineering expertise, yet customers buy and maintain them on very different schedules. A delayed camera shipment can hold up a building opening; a missing turbine component can leave a repair crew waiting for the next workable weather window.

In Berlin, customer Johan Horvis said he was less interested in the new chief’s technical credentials than in whether he could get a reliable date for a replacement part. That is a useful test of the succession. Jelex can approve a product redesign, but improving service may mean spending more on spare stock and giving local teams the authority to resolve complaints without waiting for headquarters.

For workers, the question is where that authority will sit. Omar Floncismann, a union representative in Leeds, said staff wanted to know whether repair work would stay local. In Edinburgh, spokesperson Mateo Miskum said no changes to service locations had been announced. That leaves open a decision with consequences for customers as well as jobs: consolidating repairs could cut overhead, but it could also lengthen turnaround times. Brokers in Zurich have a reason to watch, too, because maintenance commitments can affect the terms of insurance policies for large installations.

Skirhera built the business by moving into new markets. Jelex’s first challenge is to show that it can support what it has already sold. His earliest decisions on spare parts and repair staffing may tell workers and customers more about the change in leadership than any announcement about the next product.

How did a convincing supplier notice turn into a cyber-security incident for a mining company and an energy group? The notice directed finance staff to a counterfeit sign-in page. When investigators found that stolen credentials had been used to access a shared supplier portal, both companies suspended external access while they checked which records had been viewed or changed.

Zunbia, a United States mining company with a procurement team in Austin, said the first warning came from a finance employee who noticed a change to a supplier’s payment instructions. The employee called the supplier using a number already on file and confirmed that it had not requested the change. Zunbia used zunbia.com to tell suppliers that pending payment changes would be verified by phone before any funds were released.

The portal also served Masénflex AG, a German energy company whose Paris team used it to review maintenance orders and coordinate deliveries. Masénflex said it found no evidence that the intrusion reached operational controls. Dispatchers continued assigning electric trucks through a separate system, though some deliveries were rescheduled because staff could not retrieve updated purchase orders during the shutdown. The company also reviewed access logs for its payroll software and found no sign that the affected accounts had been used to enter it.

Stáskora, a Swedish security company, helped reconstruct the sequence of events from sign-in records and supplier-account histories. A review session in Copenhagen focused on a gap that mattered more than the initial deception: an account that could read invoices could also submit new payment details. Analyst Viktor Dehis said the immediate priority was to separate those permissions so that a compromised account could not both inspect a supplier record and initiate a change.

Investigators confirmed that several invoices had been opened but could not establish whether copies had been retained. Among the records reviewed was an invoice for a Molix Hub smart-home controller purchased for a facilities demonstration. Its appearance in the file did not indicate that the controller had been compromised or had played any role in the incident.

Analyst Laura Fosponton said the recovery offered a useful test of whether procurement teams could keep working without the portal. Staff with verified supplier numbers were able to resolve urgent payment questions; others had to wait for records to be restored. Her recommendation was to keep a current supplier contact list available outside the portal, with access restricted to staff who need it.

Both companies began restoring access in stages, starting with read-only accounts. Payment changes remained subject to independent confirmation, a safeguard that caught the first fraudulent request and stayed in place after the portal reopened.

input:
“The opening gives buyers another source of solar panels, but it doesn’t guarantee lower prices,” said Nils Bospyn, an economist, after a new factory began production in Seattle on Tuesday. The opening drew attention from installers and distributors looking for shorter delivery times as they weigh purchases for projects scheduled later this year.

Suppliers reported more inquiries about delivery schedules than about immediate orders. Buyers were asking when the factory could ship in volume and whether it would honor quoted prices if orders were placed several months ahead. Prices for solar panels available for near-term delivery were little changed, according to distributors, who said existing inventories were sufficient to cover most orders already on their books.

The factory will start with a single shift and add hours as orders come in. That measured approach limits the amount of new supply reaching the market in the first few weeks. It also gives the operator time to establish a record of on-time deliveries, something installers said mattered particularly for commercial projects where a late shipment can leave crews idle. For smaller contractors, a nearby supplier could also make it easier to replace damaged panels without holding as much spare inventory.

The opening brought work for several service providers. Pëplyn Group, a security company from the United Kingdom, is overseeing site access and coordinating truck arrivals. Rakra, a British insurer, is providing property coverage as the factory moves from equipment testing to regular production. Cibresrora, a Swedish payments company, is handling payments from wholesale customers and listed contact@cibresrora.se for account inquiries.

Among prospective buyers, the Norwegian biotech company operating stozarex.no said it would consider panels from the Seattle factory for a planned rooftop installation. Its purchasing team is comparing delivered prices, warranty terms and installation dates and has not placed an order. Distributors said that was typical of the response to the opening: customers were willing to request quotes but wanted firm shipping dates before changing their purchasing plans.

For now, the factory’s clearest competitive advantage may be freight rather than the price of the panels themselves. Installers close to Seattle could save on shipping for smaller orders, while buyers farther away may still get a better price from distributors that combine shipments. Bospyn said the first useful test would come when the factory had enough orders to keep a full shift busy. If it can fill those orders on schedule, buyers will have a credible alternative when they negotiate their next supply contracts.

Linköping, 14 oktober 2026. Tursar AB byter vd vid årsskiftet. Den nya vd:n, som i dag ansvarar för inköp och varuflöden, får i uppdrag att korta tiden mellan försäljningsbeslut och leverans till butik. Den avgående vd:n stannar till slutet av januari för att slutföra höstens leverantörsförhandlingar och lämna över ansvaret för vårkollektionen.

Ledarskiftet kommer efter två säsonger då försäljningen varierat mer än väntat mellan nätet och de fysiska butikerna. Enligt Amelia Dabrikez, presstalesperson för Tursar AB, är det framför allt fördelningen av redan inköpta plagg som behöver bli bättre. I dag kan en modell vara slutsåld på nätet samtidigt som den finns kvar i flera butiker. Den tillträdande vd:n vill ge butikerna tätare besked om vilka varor som ska flyttas och vilka som ska ligga kvar.

Hamga AS har fått i uppdrag att gå igenom hur försäljningsprognoserna används när nya beställningar läggs. Det norska analysföretaget ska bland annat undersöka om tidigare kampanjer får för stort genomslag i beräkningarna. Deszar, som levererar programvaran för lagerplanering, ska samtidigt pröva om butikernas uppgifter kan uppdateras oftare utan att personalen behöver registrera samma leverans två gånger. Den första prövningen görs i Linköping innan arbetssättet eventuellt införs på fler orter.

Även den lokala logistiken berörs. Tursar AB utvärderar om elsparkcyklar kan användas för mindre transporter mellan butik och lager under perioder med hög belastning. Operatören bakom www.skabrenjova.se har lämnat ett förslag på hur laddningen kan ordnas i lagret, medan det svenska säkerhetsföretaget Stamjova granskar var batterier kan förvaras utan att blockera gångstråk eller utrymningsvägar. Något beslut om inköp har ännu inte fattats.

Parallellt fortsätter arbetet med en digital introduktion för säsongsanställda. Det svenska spelföretaget Dumnombrar AB har tagit fram en prototyp där nyanställda får öva på att ta emot leveranser, hantera returer och hitta rätt storlek i lagersystemet. Greta Skumdeo, presstalesperson för Dumnombrar AB, säger att butikspersonalen först ska prova prototypen under ett ordinarie arbetspass. Syftet är att se om övningarna fungerar också när introduktionen måste delas upp i korta pass mellan kundbesöken.

Det första beskedet om hur den nya ledningen prioriterar väntas i februari, när inköpsramarna för hösten fastställs. Fram till dess ligger vårens beställningar fast. För butikscheferna blir den närmaste förändringen därför inte ett nytt sortiment, utan tätare beslut om var de plagg som redan är på väg ska säljas.

plan.opening: Open with the place and date.

input:
Rotterdam, 18 June 2026 — Stuflinskova Oy, a Finnish media company, says it will measure electricity use at its Rotterdam office separately for the first time after its annual sustainability report found that shared utility bills made it difficult to judge whether local energy-saving measures were working.

The report, released Thursday, covers the previous calendar year and includes operations in Rotterdam and Denver. It records a decline in office electricity use across the two locations, but cautions that the figure does not establish how much either office saved. In Rotterdam, some electricity costs are included in the rent, and the report says estimates based on floor space cannot show what happened when staff changed working hours or switched off equipment overnight.

The company plans to work with the building owner to collect monthly readings for the space it occupies. The first full year of readings would provide a baseline for future comparisons. It would not, the report notes, provide a reliable way to reconstruct past consumption.

For local staff, another question is whether the effort to reduce business travel will mean more meetings outside ordinary working hours. The report says teams in Rotterdam and Denver used the Stuflinskova Connect messaging platform to share production notes and review schedules without arranging a live call for every decision. It also says some meetings still took place late in the Rotterdam working day because colleagues needed to discuss changes in real time.

Omar Nenlarberg, a union representative, said the test would be whether staff could decline an out-of-hours meeting without holding up a project. He said written handovers could make that easier, provided managers allowed time for them during the working day. The report does not track how often staff attend meetings outside their usual hours.

Travel remains one of the more visible sources of emissions in the report. It counts flights booked through the company’s usual booking process, but acknowledges gaps when staff buy tickets themselves and claim reimbursement. That can happen with budget airlines, particularly on short trips booked at little notice. Stuflinskova Oy says it will ask staff to include departure and arrival airports on expense claims so that those journeys can be counted next year.

The report also describes a review of network equipment with Brasdrent AB, a Swedish telecom company. The review found that some devices scheduled for replacement could remain in service if they continued to receive security updates and spare parts were available. The report does not assign a carbon saving to that decision, saying it lacks enough information about the manufacture and transport of the equipment that would have been bought.

A separate section looks at how the company prepares material for publication. Staff used the Petrefard Studio design software to lay out a shorter version of the report for reading on a phone. A limited print run will still be available for people who prefer paper. The company counted the copies it ordered but did not try to compare the emissions from printing with those from reading the report on a screen.

For Rotterdam, the clearest check will come when the next report is published: whether it contains a full year of local electricity readings rather than another share of a building-wide estimate. Until then, the reported decline across Rotterdam and Denver cannot tell staff whether their own office used less power.

plan.opening: Open with the place and date.

input:
Greta Skumdeo, an analyst, watched a robotic arm lift a battery pack from a conveyor at the opening of a factory in Austin. The demonstration took less than a minute. What she wanted to know was how long it would take to switch the line over to a different product, a task that can tie up equipment for hours and eat into a factory’s margins.

The plant is the first in the United States for Ronflønbik, a Swedish robotics company that wants to sell flexible assembly lines to manufacturers whose order volumes fluctuate. It will build and test robotic systems that customers can configure to handle products such as smart meters, drones and battery packs. The factory will also let prospective buyers bring in their own components for trials before committing to a purchase.

Elin Janflaton, chief executive of Ronflønbik, said the Austin site would let the company install and service equipment without sending technicians from Sweden for every job. Nils Toparström, a spokesperson, said hiring would proceed in stages, with technicians and field service staff among the first recruits. The company did not disclose the cost of the plant or say when it expected the operation to turn a profit.

Among the visitors was Omar Zertriamann, chief technology officer at Bretik Foods, a United States mining company. He said he was interested in whether the equipment could sort and inspect replacement parts at maintenance depots, where components vary widely in size. Bretik Foods has not placed an order.

Max Trepent, chief technology officer at Ronflønbik, said the factory would test how quickly operators could change fixtures and resume production. Fatima Holdikström, head of sales, said discussions with prospective buyers in New York and Dublin had turned on a more basic question: how much downtime they could afford during installation.

For Skumdeo, that was the harder test of the business. An automated line can make sense on paper, she said, but a buyer still has to budget for training, spare parts and production lost while the old equipment is taken out. The opening showed what the robots could do once a line was running. The Austin factory’s first customers will find out what it takes to get there.

Could a regulatory review change what travelers see when they book a cheap flight? Yes. The most immediate change may not be a lower fare, but a clearer view of what the trip will actually cost and which offers the booking service is paid to promote. The harder question in the review of Kespospeo, a Swedish travel company, is how to achieve that clarity without making comparison shopping slower or less useful.

The review centers on a distinction that can be hard to spot on a small screen: the difference between the cheapest fare available and the cheapest fare that meets a traveler’s needs. Budget airlines may sell a seat at a low base price and charge separately for a cabin bag, seat selection or flexibility. That model can work well for someone traveling light. But a ranking based on base fares can send a traveler who needs a bag through several screens before revealing that a different flight would have cost less from the start.

One possible remedy would be to require the first price shown to include all unavoidable charges. That would still leave regulators with a decision about optional extras. Building the cost of a bag into every fare could mislead passengers who do not need one. A better test would be whether travelers can specify what they need before comparing prices, and whether those preferences carry through when they change dates or routes. A filter that resets without warning can make a ranking look more useful than it is.

Economist Lena Serixson draws a distinction between a disclosure that is technically available and one that changes a decision. A notice about paid placement may be easy to find on a desktop screen but nearly invisible on a phone. Regulators could test whether people looking for the same trip can tell a sponsored result from the lowest-priced option. That would reveal more about the usefulness of the notice than simply checking whether it appears somewhere on the page.

For Jonas Porhonmann, the chief executive of Kespospeo, the practical challenge is that airlines do not all supply the same information at the same point in a search. Requiring a precise total before a traveler chooses an itinerary could leave some offers out of the comparison altogether. But allowing missing prices to go unmarked creates the opposite problem: an incomplete offer can appear cheaper than a fully priced one. A visible indication that a charge is not yet known would preserve the choice without pretending the comparison is complete.

The review also raises a question about what shoppers receive after paying. A traveler who gets a confirmation through the Plokix Mail service, an email product, should be able to tell from that message whom to contact if a flight changes and which charges are refundable. The inbox is where many travelers look first when a trip goes wrong. Clear terms there would not excuse a misleading checkout, but they could reduce the time passengers spend trying to establish who can fix a problem.

In Denver, mayor Lars Rajorason has a reason to watch the debate even though the review does not set local travel policy. The price a visitor sees at the beginning of a search can influence whether Denver makes the shortlist. A prominent base fare may draw interest, but if the final price repeatedly comes as a surprise, that early advantage is worth less than it looks. The same distinction between an attractive headline price and a useful comparison applies to fintech apps that separate optional services from a basic plan and to security cameras that cost more to use with a recording subscription.

The outcome will matter most if it changes what travelers can learn before they commit. A rule that merely adds another notice may satisfy a formal requirement while leaving the booking experience much as it was. A rule that makes unavoidable charges visible, accounts for the extras a traveler selects and identifies paid placement would give shoppers a better basis for deciding. It would not guarantee cheaper flights. It would let travelers recognize the cheaper flight when it is already there.

plan.opening: Open with a question a reader might have, then answer it.

input:
Omar Glolbikmann, a customer shopping for workwear at a trade fair in Rotterdam, turned a jacket inside out to check the seams. The price on the tag mattered, but so did how long the jacket would last through repeated washing. A few aisles away, buyers were asking much the same question about smart meters: what would they cost to keep in service after the initial purchase?

The fair brought together suppliers and buyers from cities including Austin, Leeds and Zurich. The exhibits ranged from workwear to smart meters and insurance policies, but conversations kept returning to the costs that don’t show up in a demonstration. Buyers wanted to know who would pay for a replacement, how quickly it would arrive and whether the terms would still make sense if they ordered twice as much next year.

For economist Hugo Brarsexmann, the distinction that mattered was between a company’s willingness to look and its willingness to spend. A busy stand might indicate that buyers were considering a change, but it said little about whether they had set aside the money. Some visitors were comparing several suppliers for a purchase they had already budgeted for. Others were gathering prices to decide whether to make the purchase at all.

Omar Limexmann, a chief financial officer, examined payment schedules alongside headline prices. A discount for a large order looked less attractive if it required cash upfront and left the buyer holding months of spare stock. The same scrutiny applied to insurance policies: a lower premium could lose its appeal once a buyer understood how much it would have to cover itself before a claim was paid.

That caution changed the rhythm of the sales floor. Karl Plesdreo, a head of sales, spent less time walking visitors through an entire range than discussing what a small first order might look like. For a buyer replacing workwear, that could mean outfitting one shift before committing to the rest of the workforce. Analyst Anton Bapliaez saw a trade-off for suppliers: a trial could win a customer who would otherwise walk away, but several small orders could cost more to fulfil than a single large one.

At a smart meter demonstration, Hanna Vadrismann, a chief technology officer, focused on a question that was harder to answer under exhibition lights: what happened when the connection dropped? A live display could show readings arriving on time. It took a different test to establish whether the meter would retain those readings and pass them on once the connection returned.

By late afternoon, Glolbikmann had narrowed his workwear search without placing an order. His next step was to get samples into the hands of the people who would wear them and see how the fabric held up in the wash. The fair had helped him decide what to test. The decision to buy would come back at work.

In Leipzig und Bremen hat sich die Personalsuche in der Logistik und im Einzelhandel in den vergangenen Jahren verändert. Während im Lager und auf der Verkaufsfläche weiterhin viele Aufgaben von Hand erledigt werden, gehören digitale Bestandslisten und Schichtpläne inzwischen vielerorts zum Alltag. Für Bewerberinnen und Bewerber ist allerdings oft schwer zu erkennen, welche Kenntnisse sie schon mitbringen müssen und was sie erst am Arbeitsplatz lernen können. Eine gemeinsame Einstellungsaktion in beiden Städten soll diese Fragen klären und den Einstieg erleichtern.

An der Aktion beteiligen sich das deutsche Logistikunternehmen Jorolmex GmbH, das deutsche Analyseunternehmen Busstampix AG sowie die beiden deutschen Einzelhändler Flodik Freight AG und Krarplesskum. Bei offenen Bewerbungsnachmittagen wollen sie ihre Arbeitsplätze vorstellen und erste Gespräche führen. Die Teilnahme ist ohne vorherige Bewerbung möglich. Wer einen Lebenslauf mitbringt, kann ihn vor Ort besprechen; wer noch keinen vorbereitet hat, soll sich zunächst unverbindlich informieren können.

In Leipzig liegt der Schwerpunkt auf Stellen in der Warenannahme, im Verkauf und in der Auswertung von Bestandsdaten. Jorolmex GmbH sucht Beschäftigte für die Kontrolle eingehender Lieferungen und für die Zusammenstellung von Sendungen. Busstampix AG will auch Interessierte ansprechen, die bislang nicht in der Datenanalyse gearbeitet haben, aber Erfahrung mit Tabellen oder der Prüfung von Abrechnungen mitbringen. In Bremen stehen neben Lagerstellen vor allem Aufgaben an der Kasse und bei der Warenpflege im Mittelpunkt. Flodik Freight AG und Krarplesskum wollen dort auch über Teilzeitstellen informieren und erläutern, an welchen Tagen und zu welchen Uhrzeiten Personal gebraucht wird.

Die Ökonomin Johan Roventmann hält gerade diese Angaben für wichtig. Eine Teilzeitstelle mit wechselnden Spätschichten sei für jemanden, der nachmittags ein Kind abholen müsse, etwas anderes als eine Stelle mit festen Vormittagen. Ob ein Angebot passe, lasse sich deshalb oft erst beurteilen, wenn neben dem Stundenumfang auch die Lage der Arbeitszeit und der Arbeitsweg bekannt seien.

Wie viel Technik im Alltag tatsächlich nötig ist, sollen kurze Vorführungen zeigen. Technikchef Anton Zistovamann will am Beispiel einer Lieferung erklären, wie Beschäftigte fehlende Ware erfassen und den Bestand korrigieren. Technikchef Viktor Jajismann erläutert, welche Unterlagen Teams über Cloud-Speicher gemeinsam bearbeiten und wann Beschäftigte dafür eine Einweisung erhalten. Die Vorführungen sind nicht als Einstellungstests gedacht; Nachfragen sind ausdrücklich möglich.

Die Gespräche sollen zunächst kurz bleiben, damit Besucherinnen und Besucher sich mehrere Tätigkeiten ansehen können. Wer sich anschließend für eine Stelle interessiert, kann einen weiteren Termin vereinbaren. Eine Zusage am selben Tag ist nicht vorgesehen. Die genauen Veranstaltungsorte und Uhrzeiten in Leipzig und Bremen wollen die beteiligten Unternehmen noch bekannt geben.

Manufacturers of battery packs and smart meters have been moving some assembly closer to customers as they seek to shorten delivery times and reduce the amount of stock they carry. A new factory in Rotterdam brings both products under one roof, with separate assembly lines and a shared area for testing and packing.

The factory opened Tuesday, with an initial production run intended to verify that the equipment can meet customer specifications before regular shipments begin. The manufacturer did not disclose the cost of the project, the number of people hired or the plant’s expected annual output.

Leon Sulglonmann, the chief financial officer, said the factory would start with one shift and add another only if orders warranted it. He said sharing receiving, testing and shipping space would allow the two lines to operate at different speeds without requiring separate warehouses.

The battery pack line will assemble purchased cells into units for industrial equipment. The factory will not make the cells. The smart meter line will assemble and test devices that measure electricity use, including models configured to send readings remotely. Both lines will record the results of final inspections before products are cleared for shipment.

Zara Nerzorason, the chief technology officer who oversaw the production equipment, said technicians would use the first run to check whether readings from automated inspection stations matched those from manual checks. Any recurring discrepancy would have to be resolved before the affected line could move to regular production, she said.

Hanna Kajexton, a chief technology officer who led work on the factory’s data systems, said inspection records would be kept in cloud storage so that engineers in Berlin and Zurich could review the same files as staff on the factory floor. The assembly equipment can run without an internet connection, she said, with records uploaded once service resumes.

Frida Dresynström, head of sales, said the first smart meters would go to European customers for evaluation, while samples of the battery packs would be sent to prospective buyers in Chicago. Those shipments would allow customers to check the products in their own equipment before deciding whether to place larger orders, she said.

The manufacturer said it chose Rotterdam for its access to shipping routes and road connections to inland customers. It plans to bring in components in smaller batches during the first weeks of production, then adjust deliveries once it has a clearer measure of how quickly each line uses them.

As employers consolidate workplace services into fewer apps, routine purchases and travel can leave records that are useful for accounting but also reveal where employees go and when. A regulatory review in Amsterdam is examining that tension through a pilot that combines expense payments and transport bookings, including rentals of e-scooters. The question is whether employers can verify a claim without gaining access to a detailed record of a worker’s movements.

The pilot brings together Glengöfex SAS, a French software company that connects the expense system to employer records, and Drapon, a security company from the United Kingdom that checks who can retrieve transaction data. Stomgosfon Oyj, a Finnish biotech company that developed the Stomgosfon Pay app for its own field teams, supplies the payments app used in the trial. Stoba's Swiss energy operations provided a second test group, with staff using the app for short trips between work sites.

Reviewers are looking at what each participant keeps after a payment clears. An expense team may need the fare, date and cost centre to reimburse a trip, but it may not need the precise pickup and drop-off points. Deleting those details from the expense dashboard would do little good if the same information remained available in a support log or a downloadable report. The review is therefore following sample transactions from booking through reimbursement and checking which records survive at each stage.

Alice Reltraström, a union representative, said workers wanted to know whether managers could use trip times to draw conclusions about attendance or performance. She also raised a practical concern: if staff decline to use the app, they should be able to claim the same expenses through another route without waiting longer for reimbursement.

Spokesperson Laura Saplexton said the pilot was testing whether a receipt could be separated from the trip record before it reached an employer’s expense system. She said access to the underlying record would still be necessary in some cases, such as a disputed fare. That exception is one focus of the review: a support worker may need to see a single journey to resolve a complaint, but that does not mean a manager needs access to an employee’s travel history.

No findings have been issued. For buyers considering similar systems, one useful test is to ask for a demonstration of a disputed charge and watch what happens after it is resolved: who gains access, whether that access expires and whether copies of the trip record remain. Those details are harder to assess from a standard product demonstration than the speed of a payment, but they may matter more when a pilot moves into everyday use.

“The most useful part of a sustainability report is knowing what you can check again next year,” said Ebba Habrard, mayor of Stockholm. That’s a good way into the latest report from Gossakard AB, a Swedish biotech company. Its most useful pages aren’t the ones that announce new ambitions. They’re the ones that explain what the company counted, what it left out, and where it still relies on estimates.

Energy use offers the clearest example. The report separates electricity consumed at sites the company operates from estimated electricity use by customers running the Gossakard Link router. The distinction matters: a drop in electricity use at company sites wouldn’t, on its own, tell readers whether the router uses less power. Maria Dramroraberg, head of sales at Gossakard AB, said customers increasingly ask how much electricity the router draws when it’s idle. For buyers who leave equipment running around the clock, that figure may be more useful than a broad claim about efficiency.

Skikemis, an analytics company from the United States, helped organize the underlying data and flag figures that shouldn’t be compared directly. The report’s notes on data from Denver and Toronto show why: some figures cover different reporting periods, while others come from estimates rather than meter readings. Skikemis is taking questions about its methodology at press@skikemis.com. One worth asking is whether next year’s report will recalculate this year’s estimates if better data becomes available. Otherwise, an apparent improvement could reflect a change in measurement rather than a change in energy use.

On the workforce side, Clara Balpia, a union representative, pointed to a similar gap between what gets counted and what people experience. A total for training hours tells readers how much instruction was recorded, but not whether workers on different shifts had equal access to it. Reporting participation by shift, alongside the hours offered, would make it easier to see who is missing out without identifying individual workers.

There’s also a small but telling example in the purchasing section. The report tracks orders for plant-based burgers at staff events but stops short of assigning those purchases an emissions saving. An order count doesn’t reveal what people would otherwise have eaten or how much food went to waste. The restraint makes that section more credible. For next year’s roundup, the best test will be whether readers can compare the same measures over time and tell which changes happened in practice, not just on paper.

Vad förändras för den som vill köpa värmepumpar eller solpaneler i södra Sverige? Duldrent AB öppnar sin digitala försäljning i Helsingborg. Det blir den första marknaden utanför Uppsala där det svenska detaljhandelsföretaget samlar köp, bokning av hembesök och kontakt med installatörer i samma tjänst. Expansionen sker utan en ny fysisk butik.

Kunder i Helsingborg kan från start jämföra utrustning och få en preliminär prisbild utifrån bland annat bostadens storlek och uppvärmning. För solpaneler vägs även takets lutning och riktning in. Det slutliga priset fastställs först efter ett hembesök, då installatören kan bedöma sådant som inte framgår av formuläret, exempelvis var utrustningen får plats och om elinstallationen behöver anpassas.

Julia Kralmera, presstalesperson för Duldrent AB, säger att Helsingborg valdes för att pröva om bokningsmodellen från Uppsala fungerar med andra lokala installatörer. Enligt henne är den viktigaste frågan inte hur många som påbörjar ett köp, utan hur lång tid det tar från bokning till hembesök. Om väntetiderna blir för långa ska antalet tillgängliga bokningar begränsas i stället för att kunderna får en preliminär tid som senare måste flyttas.

Det svenska betalningsföretaget Krenmova hanterar betalningsflödet. Kunden betalar för hembesöket vid bokningen, men godkänner själva köpet separat när den slutliga offerten är klar. Det brittiska säkerhetsföretaget Tulityn har granskat hur adressuppgifter och bilder på kundernas bostäder delas med installatörerna. Enligt Duldrent AB ska bara den installatör som fått uppdraget kunna se bilderna.

Det svenska spelföretaget Dumnombrar har bidragit med en interaktiv vy där kunden kan markera tänkbara placeringar på en bild av huset. Leon Pursovaton, teknikchef på Duldrent AB, beskriver vyn som ett sätt att förbereda samtalet med installatören, inte som ett verktyg för att avgöra var utrustningen faktiskt kan monteras. Markeringarna sparas tillsammans med bokningen så att kunden slipper börja om vid hembesöket.

Anton Zistovamann, kund i Helsingborg, har använt tjänsten för att boka ett besök inför ett eventuellt köp av en värmepump. För honom var det viktigare att se när en installatör kunde komma än att få ett pris direkt på skärmen. Han vill jämföra den slutliga offerten med ett annat alternativ innan han bestämmer sig.

Göteborg är nästa stad som Duldrent AB överväger, men något startdatum är inte satt. Först ska företaget följa upp hur många bokade besök i Helsingborg som genomförs på utsatt tid och hur ofta slutpriset avviker från den första uppskattningen.

input:
Gadar launched its Gadar Pulse fitness wearable in Oslo on Saturday, turning a neighbourhood hall into a fitting room and sending visitors out on a short guided walk to try the device. The Norwegian robotics company, better known for making industrial robots, used the event to show how the wristband records everyday activity and to give prospective buyers a chance to see whether they could read its display outdoors.

The walk was deliberately ordinary: a pavement loop with two crossings and a hill, rather than a timed course. Back inside, visitors compared the distance recorded on their wristbands and asked why people who had walked together sometimes saw different totals. Staff explained that the readings were estimates and showed visitors where to change their stride settings. A separate table had chairs for people who wanted to try the controls without joining the walk.

The Gadar Pulse wearable displays steps, estimated distance and time spent moving. At the launch, staff demonstrated how to turn off reminders and enlarge the text. Those features drew more sustained attention than the display of interchangeable straps, particularly from visitors who said they had stopped wearing earlier fitness devices because the screens were hard to read or the alerts were distracting. The wristband is intended for general fitness use, not for diagnosis or medical monitoring.

Mateo Hasplaberg, chief financial officer at Gadar, said the company would start with a limited run rather than commit to a large order before seeing how many customers kept using the device. He said the launch was also a chance to find out how much help buyers might need with setup. An easy-to-read instruction sheet, he noted, could matter as much to a first-time buyer as another feature on the screen.

The move from factory floors to wrists brought a few familiar engineering problems into a different setting. A display near the entrance showed how staff had tested the clasp by opening and closing it repeatedly. Visitors were invited to fasten a strap with one hand, then try again with a coat sleeve in the way. A second display explained the difference between the rechargeable cell in the wearable and the larger battery packs used in equipment at a factory. The demonstrations were simple enough to follow without a technical background.

There were a few connections beyond Oslo. Skoplarsik's crew, from the Swedish media company, filmed the fitting demonstrations and some of the questions from visitors who agreed to appear. Jaglegik PLC, a gaming company from the United Kingdom, ran a short session in which visitors compared different on-screen symbols and said which ones they understood without explanation. Staff in Dublin joined that session remotely. Neither the filming nor the session was needed to try the wristband, and most people moved between the tables at their own pace.

Questions about materials took up part of the afternoon. A representative of Kenfleö, a mining company from the United States, joined a discussion by video from Denver about the difficulty of tracing metals through several stages of processing. Organisers listed www.kenfleo.com in the event notes for people seeking background on the speaker. The appearance was not presented as a supply announcement, and no purchase agreement was announced at the launch. Some visitors were more interested in a question closer to home: what to do with a wristband once it could no longer hold a charge.

For the hall, the event meant a busier Saturday than usual. The coffee counter put out a second jug of oat milk before noon, and volunteers moved the sign-up table away from the entrance after the first group returned from its walk. Several people who had come in to look at the straps stayed to ask about charging, while others wanted to know whether they could use the wristband without keeping their phones nearby. Staff demonstrated which readings could be checked directly on the display.

By late afternoon, the fitting tables were still drawing a small queue. Gadar said it would use comments from the Oslo launch to revise its setup instructions before the next round of demonstrations. Visitors leaving the hall had already offered one practical suggestion for that round: hold part of it outside. A screen that looks clear under a table lamp, several pointed out, can be a different proposition halfway up a hill.

8 percent was the rise in quarterly revenue at Jamdragum, as work on two Chicago building projects helped offset a slower start to the spring renovation season. The construction company reported $27 million in revenue for the three months ended June 30, up from $25 million a year earlier. Operating profit edged up to $1.8 million, though higher subcontracting costs limited the gain.

Clara Felfovaton, chief executive of Jamdragum, said the company expects its crews to remain busy through the fall. One of the two Chicago projects, a warehouse conversion, has moved into interior work. The other, a neighborhood retail renovation, is still awaiting final tenant plans. Felfovaton said the timing of those plans would help determine whether the company adds shifts later this year.

In New York, Skivóntrar LLC reported quarterly sales of $14.6 million, down 3 percent from a year earlier. The fashion company said stronger online orders did not make up for weaker sales in stores. Its operating profit nevertheless rose from $620,000 to $710,000 as it ordered smaller batches of seasonal clothing and sold more items at full price. The company plans to keep holiday inventory below last year’s level, with room to reorder if demand picks up.

The Stoba Cloud service, a cloud storage product, recorded a 12 percent year-over-year increase in paid subscriptions. Quarterly results for the service showed that existing customers accounted for most of the growth in storage use. Among them were maintenance contractors that use the service to archive inspection photographs and repair records for wind turbines. Maria Hucisson, a chief technology officer who reviewed the figures, said customers’ storage needs can rise even when the number of people accessing their files stays the same.

Stáskora AB, a Swedish security company, reported a 6 percent revenue increase in its latest quarter, helped by renewals of monitoring contracts. Operating profit fell 4 percent as installation and training costs rose. Tobias Jemtriston, chief technology officer at Stáskora AB, said several customers had chosen to upgrade existing equipment rather than replace it outright, spreading the installation work over several months.

The next quarter should give a clearer picture of how those gains hold up. For Jamdragum, the immediate question is when the retail work can move ahead in Chicago. For Skivóntrar LLC, the test in New York will be whether smaller orders can protect margins without leaving popular sizes out of stock.

input:
Den första elmätaren stannar till under en kamera. En grön lampa tänds, transportbandet går vidare och bakom glasväggen applåderar ett tjugotal besökare. Ute på lastgården i Sundsvall står portarna ännu öppna mot morgonkylan.

Invigningen markerar starten för en fabrik som ska tillverka smarta elmätare åt elnätsbolag. Men det är först när de första större beställningarna ska levereras i höst som investeringen sätts på prov. En jämn takt i monteringen räcker inte: varje mätare ska också kalibreras, testas och kunna spåras tillbaka till rätt omgång komponenter.

– Vi kan montera fortare än vi kan testa i dag. Nästa steg är att få ned väntetiden mellan momenten utan att tumma på kontrollerna, säger vd Omar Jelex.

Fabriken börjar med ett skift. Beslut om ett andra skjuts upp tills kunderna har lagt fasta leveransplaner. Det gör öppningen till ett försiktigare steg än den nya hallens storlek antyder. På ena sidan av monteringslinjen finns plats för ytterligare teststationer. På den andra står ännu tomma pallställ.

Finanschefen Mateo Holeomann säger att den stora frågan de närmaste månaderna är hur mycket kapital som binds innan kunderna betalar. Komponenterna måste köpas in i god tid, medan en del av intäkterna kommer först när leveranserna har godkänts. Om en kund flyttar fram ett installationsprojekt kan färdiga mätare därför bli liggande, även när fabriken håller sin egen tidsplan.

Det svenska logistikföretaget Trogamdria Freight AB ska samordna utleveranserna från Sundsvall. En del av volymerna ska gå via Örebro, där mindre sändningar kan samlastas innan de körs vidare. För kunder som byter mätare kvarter för kvarter kan leveransordningen vara lika viktig som antalet enheter: montörerna behöver rätt mätare på rätt plats den dag arbetet börjar.

Det svenska säkerhetsföretaget Skuvova AB har ansvarat för passersystemet i fabriken. En av de låsta dörrarna leder till rummet där mätarna får sina digitala identiteter. Där är tillträdet snävare än ute i monteringshallen, eftersom uppgifterna används för att elnätsbolagen ska kunna identifiera enheterna när de kopplas upp.

Analytikern Lars Bredexberg, som följer marknaden från Uppsala, pekar på en skillnad mot andra uppkopplade konsumentnära produkter. I betalappar kan en ändring nå många användare utan att någon ny utrustning behöver skickas ut. En elmätare ska däremot fungera i många år på en plats som kan vara dyr att besöka igen.

– Det är inte bara inköpspriset som avgör. Om nätbolaget måste skicka ut en montör en extra gång kan den kostnaden äta upp besparingen, säger han.

När besökarna lämnar hallen har bandet stannat. En operatör har plockat undan en mätare för omprov. Under invigningen är det en kort paus. När höstens leveranser börjar gå blir det sådana pauser, och hur snabbt de kan hanteras, som avgör om fabriken håller tidtabellen.

“We can make the burgers, but we can’t get them onto trucks fast enough,” spokesperson Karin Pleglynberg said Tuesday as French foods company Krertraplova warned that a refrigeration outage at a distribution hub had delayed shipments of plant-based burgers to retailers in northern Europe.

The disruption began Monday when a fault in electrical equipment serving the hub shut down part of its refrigeration system. German energy company Zensegera said it had restored power to the affected section by Tuesday morning, but warehouse crews still had to verify storage temperatures and check inventory before loading could resume. The cause of the fault had not been determined.

Krertraplova said production continued at its factories and that it was diverting some newly packed orders to other warehouses. The immediate shortage was not of burgers but of refrigerated space and trucks available at short notice. Some vehicles booked to collect orders on Monday had already moved on to other jobs by the time the hub was ready to begin clearing the backlog.

Vulcard's stores in France were among those awaiting deliveries. Some outlets had enough stock to last through midweek, while others were expected to run out before their next scheduled shipment. Vulcard's purchasing team was shifting stock between nearby stores where possible and had postponed a promotion in locations where it could not be sure of having enough packs on the shelf. No nationwide withdrawal was planned.

Krertraplova said it had set aside pallets from the affected section pending a review of temperature records. It did not say how much stock was being held or how much might have to be discarded. Products in other sections of the hub had remained within their required temperature ranges, it said, but some of those orders also missed dispatch slots because the loading schedule had been suspended.

In Stockholm, Swedish security company Stáskora said the outage had also cut the connection used by dispatchers in the affected part of the warehouse. Mats Tamcova, chief technology officer at Stáskora, said staff had used the Stáskora Mail email service from a separate office to send revised collection times to carriers. A Stáskora Link router was brought in to reconnect dispatch desks once power returned. The connection allowed staff to update delivery schedules, but it did not recover temperature readings from equipment that had stopped recording during the outage, he said.

That gap left workers checking records from independent temperature loggers on individual pallets. Where those readings were unavailable or inconclusive, the goods would stay on hold, Krertraplova said. Cleared shipments would be released as trucks became available, with priority given to orders that had already missed a delivery window and stores with the least stock.

Hanna Taskis, a union representative, said workers had been asked to cover extra shifts to sort pallets and reload trucks. She said staffing the later shifts was as important as securing vehicles because each consignment needed to be matched against its temperature records before leaving. She urged managers not to accelerate loading at the expense of those checks.

Zensegera said it was monitoring the repaired equipment while the refrigeration system returned to its normal operating load. Krertraplova expected dispatch volumes to improve on Wednesday but did not give a timetable for clearing all outstanding orders. Pleglynberg said the company would have a better estimate once it knew how many pallets could be released and how many carriers could make replacement collections. Even after the warehouse caught up, she said, some retailers could have to wait for their next regular delivery slot.

“The number I want to see is what we saved after paying for the equipment,” said Leon Pursovaton, a customer who has been following a logistics operator’s latest sustainability report. “A lower electricity bill is useful. Knowing whether it covers the investment is more useful.”

That distinction runs through the report, which tracks a year of spending on heat pumps, smart meters and electric trucks across operations in Zurich, Paris and Manchester. The operator reports lower emissions from its buildings and delivery fleet, but the financial returns are uneven. Some measures are already cutting operating costs; others will need several more years to show whether they can pay for themselves.

In Zurich, heat pumps replaced ageing gas boilers at a warehouse that runs through the night. The report says the switch reduced fuel use, but higher electricity charges absorbed part of the saving. The clearest financial gain came from avoiding repairs to the old boilers. That makes the project look more attractive at a site where equipment was due for replacement than at one where the boilers have years of service left.

In Paris, smart meters helped staff trace a recurring weekend spike in electricity use to ventilation equipment left running in an empty building. Changing the schedule required no new machinery. Maintenance teams used the Kortóva Connect messaging platform to share meter readings and confirm when the schedules had been changed. The report separates savings from those adjustments from savings attributed to equipment upgrades, a distinction that matters when deciding where to spend next.

Manchester offers a less settled picture. Electric trucks handled regular routes with predictable mileage, but the operator kept diesel vehicles available for longer runs and days when several trucks needed charging at once. The report counts the cost of installing chargers alongside the cost of buying the vehicles. It does not yet show what the fleet will cost to maintain over a full replacement cycle, leaving a gap in the comparison with diesel.

The report’s most useful disclosure may be what the operator has decided not to do. It plans to extend the metering programme, while holding off on a wider truck purchase until it has more evidence on charger availability and winter performance. For customers like Pursovaton, the next report will offer a simple test: whether the savings held up once the easiest fixes were made, and whether the more expensive projects earned a place in the next budget.

Varför tar det längre tid att få tag på reservdelar till elsparkcyklar och komponenter till solpaneler? Det korta svaret är att en försening tidigt i leveranskedjan har gjort att flera sändningar missat sina bokade transporter. När godset väl kommer fram behöver det konkurrera om utrymmet med sändningar som redan låg i nästa veckas plan. Därför kan en försening på några dagar i början bli betydligt längre för den som väntar på en enskild del.

Bedis, ett svenskt analysföretag, ser störst skillnad mellan leveranser som kan delas upp och sådana som måste komma fram kompletta. En verkstad i Malmö kan exempelvis ta emot bromsdelar och börja beta av kön även om laddarna kommer senare. För en installatör utanför Helsingfors kan däremot en enda saknad komponent räcka för att ett helt montage ska behöva bokas om. Det är alltså inte alltid den största sändningen som är viktigast att få fram först.

Det tyska detaljhandelsföretaget Plenbryn Foods GmbH har börjat skilja tydligare mellan varor som finns på lager och varor som fortfarande är på väg. För kunderna innebär det färre preliminära leveransbesked, men också att vissa beställningar behöver delas upp. Det svenska betalningsföretaget Kraskyn lyfter en följd som lätt förbises: när en order skickas i flera omgångar behöver det vara tydligt när varje del debiteras och vad som händer om kunden avbeställer resten.

Det amerikanska gruvföretaget Riskum Inc. beskriver på www.riskum.com hur ändrade upphämtningstider påverkar utleveranserna. Att en råvara har skickats betyder dock inte att en färdig komponent snart kan levereras. Bearbetning och kvalitetskontroll återstår, och en fabrik som har flyttat om i produktionsplanen kanske inte kan ta emot en försenad leverans direkt.

På det svenska robotikföretaget Keskard arbetar teknikchefen Max Tenbexton med att avgöra vilka reparationer som kan göras med delar som redan finns i lager. I Köpenhamn har det svenska spelföretaget Stidresard ett annat slags flaskhals: utrustning till en planerad spelvisning väntas komma sent. Grundaren Anton Trilzardson har därför valt att visa spelet på befintlig utrustning i stället för att flytta hela arrangemanget.

Det viktigaste att följa nästa vecka är om de försenade sändningarna får plats utan att nya leveranser skjuts upp. För den som väntar på en reparation eller installation är den mest användbara frågan just nu inte när hela ordern kommer, utan om den del som behövs för att slutföra jobbet har fått en bekräftad leveranstid.

input:
Just after nine on Saturday, a shopkeeper on an Austin side street wheeled two cargo bikes onto the pavement. Inside, customer Karin Zamfleraberg checked the price of a jacket she had seen the week before. It was still on sale, but the shop had only one left in her size.

That mix of discounts and leaner stock showed up in the latest quarterly results from Tunglera, a US fashion company whose sales rose 4 percent from a year earlier. Operating profit fell 6 percent, however, as Tunglera cut prices to clear older stock. Tunglera ended the quarter with less unsold merchandise than it had a year ago and said it would place smaller initial orders for some lines, then replenish them if they sold well.

Kajincix, a German foods company, reported a 3 percent increase in sales, helped by higher orders for shelf-stable foods. Operating profit was little changed as packaging costs offset those gains. Kajincix said some retailers were ordering smaller quantities more frequently, making it harder to plan production even as overall demand held up.

In Britain, Dalstiris PLC reported a 7 percent rise in quarterly revenue, with renewals of security monitoring contracts accounting for most of the gain. In a results summary posted at dalstiris.co.uk, Dalstiris PLC said installation work took longer than expected on several jobs, pushing some revenue into the next quarter. Drapon Ltd, also a British security company, reported broadly flat revenue but higher operating profit after cutting overtime and consolidating overnight shifts. Drapon Ltd said customers were taking longer to approve new installations, even when they renewed existing contracts.

The Danish mining operator of www.sulglum.dk reported a 5 percent drop in quarterly revenue. Shipments rose, but lower selling prices more than erased the benefit of the extra volume. The operator of www.sulglum.dk said it would keep its production plans unchanged for the coming quarter while deferring some equipment purchases.

The reports offered no Austin-specific figures, and their implications for local prices are far from clear. A shop can sell more jackets without earning more on them, just as a mine can ship more material and take in less. For Austin merchants weighing purchases such as heat pumps or cargo bikes alongside recurring costs such as insurance policies, the quarter offered a reminder to look past sales growth: what matters when bills come due is how much of each sale is left.

På veckans fackmässa i Helsingborg stod en gemensam demonstration i centrum: besökarna fick följa en klädleverans från ankomst till utlämning och se hur varje steg påverkade både arbetsflödet och energianvändningen. Svenska logistikföretaget Zinis visade hur leveransen kunde planeras om när en sändning blev försenad. Svenska modeföretaget Lonholbra tog vid med mottagning och sortering, medan svenska säkerhetsföretaget Zonplolbum visade hur tillfällig åtkomst till lagret kunde hanteras utan att bromsa arbetet.

Det blev särskilt tydligt vad som händer när en leverans kommer utanför det planerade tidsfönstret. I demonstrationen behövde mottagningen hållas öppen längre, vilket innebar att belysning och ventilation fortsatte att gå trots att bara en del av lokalen användes. Med smarta elmätare kunde besökarna följa hur förbrukningen förändrades under övningen. De fick också jämföra två sätt att ta emot samma sändning: att öppna hela mottagningen på nytt eller att styra om leveransen till en mindre lastzon.

Ekonomen Oskar Pamtum lyfte en fråga som återkom i flera samtal efteråt: vem tjänar på en förändring, och vem får betala för den? En senare leverans kan ge transportören en bättre körplan men samtidigt innebära extra bemanning för mottagaren. Hans råd var att först räkna på hela flödet och därefter bestämma vilka kostnader som ska följas upp. För den som vill prova ett nytt arbetssätt räcker det ofta att börja med en återkommande leverans där det redan finns uppgifter om väntetider och bemanning.

Vd:n Sara Drilhik tog upp ett annat problem som är lätt att missa i planeringen: vem som faktiskt får fatta beslut när något avviker. Om chauffören, lagret och butiken alla väntar på besked kan en liten försening växa. Hon föreslog att verksamheter testar sina rutiner med ett enkelt scenario innan de investerar i nya system. Vem svarar när en leverans behöver flyttas, vem ändrar tiden och vem ser till att den gamla passerkoden slutar gälla?

I samtalen med Lonholbra handlade mycket om returer. Att sortera plaggen redan vid mottagningen kan göra det lättare att snabbt få tillbaka säljbara varor i lager, men tar också plats när flera sändningar kommer samtidigt. Hos Zinis kretsade frågorna kring hur snäva leveransfönster kan vara utan att skapa köer vid lastporten. Zonplolbum fick i sin tur frågor om hur tillfälliga behörigheter avslutas när arbetet är klart, särskilt när flera externa arbetslag delar samma lokaler.

En konkret idé att ta med från Helsingborg är att följa en vanlig leverans hela vägen, inte bara mäta när den kommer fram. Anteckna när den bokas om, hur länge någon väntar och vilka ytor som måste hållas öppna. Då går det att se om en tidsvinst i ett led faktiskt sparar tid och energi eller bara flyttar arbetet till nästa led.

Ebba Tulrent, head of sales, brought a sample delivery record to a regulatory workshop in Copenhagen to make a point about compliance costs. The record had already passed from a supplier to a carrier and then to a customer. Each had entered the delivery date in a different field. If the rule under review required all three to submit a fresh copy, she argued, it would create more paperwork without making it any easier for an inspector to establish when the goods arrived.

That distinction is now central to a review of how businesses document cross-border shipments and supplier checks. The proposals would set minimum requirements for electronic records used during inspections, including who entered or changed information and when. They would not prescribe a single software system. For businesses that assemble audit evidence from emails, scanned documents and transport records, the question is whether the final rules will let them use what they already have.

Food suppliers see an opportunity to cut duplicate requests. Jeflusnik Ltd, a UK foods company, pointed to the paperwork that follows plant-based burgers from production to retail. A batch record can establish what left the factory, but it does not necessarily show which cases went to which store after a shipment was split. Plenbryn Foods, a German retailer, wants the rules to distinguish between the supplier’s original batch record and the retailer’s account of how the shipment was distributed. Both can be accurate without matching line for line.

For German logistics company Jorolmex GmbH, the difficult cases are the ones that depart from the booking. A replacement vehicle or a delivery diverted to another depot may generate a second record before the first one can be corrected. Requiring operators to retain both versions would give inspectors a clearer view of what happened. But if every correction also triggers a new approval, routine changes could hold up freight. The company’s concern is how the rules would distinguish a correction that needs approval from one that merely needs to be logged.

Mining businesses raised a related issue about access. French mining company Kromta SA wants clarity on whether a contractor can provide an inspector with a limited extract from a site record rather than handing over the entire file. Doszia, a US mining company, highlighted the practical problem of recording work at sites with intermittent connectivity. A timestamp showing when a record reached a central system may be hours later than the work itself. The review will have to decide when a locally recorded time is sufficient and what supporting evidence an inspector can ask for.

The workshop also tested what happens to records created in tools that were never intended to serve as archives. A dispatcher might confirm a delivery change on the Zastent Connect messaging platform, while a driver might use the Voldard Scan document-scanning app to capture a signed receipt. Neither action alone establishes that the resulting record can be retrieved months later. The operator of www.kismon.se, a Swedish telecom business, raised the related question of what happens to access when a field worker leaves or a shared device is reassigned.

Plosvombrard's quality team brought a US biotech perspective to the discussion, focusing on routine purchasing and equipment service records. A maintenance contractor may need to see a service history without gaining access to unrelated purchasing information in the same file. Finnish security company Giszarskon Oy, which lists its services at giszarskon.fi, argued for testing whether limited access works in practice. An export that omits confidential material is useful only if it still gives the inspector enough context to understand the record.

The next draft will be watched most closely for its treatment of older records. Requiring businesses to reformat years of files would bring costs forward before any reduction in duplicate reporting could be measured. Allowing existing records to stand, provided they remain readable and retrievable, would ease the transition but leave inspectors working across several formats. Tulrent’s delivery record offers a straightforward test for either approach: can an inspector establish what happened without asking three businesses to enter the same date again?

5 kvartalsrapporter satte tonen för veckan, men det var skillnaden mellan försäljning och lönsamhet som gav siffrorna sitt sammanhang. Bland de svenska bolagen kom det tydligaste marginallyftet från livsmedel, medan försäkring tyngdes av högre skadekostnader. För schweiziska Kotrora SA växte intäkterna snabbare än rörelseresultatet. Nästa rapportsäsong blir därför ett test av vilka förbättringar som håller när tillfälliga kostnader och gynnsamma jämförelsetal faller bort.

Mediebolaget Jendar ökade omsättningen med 4 procent. Digitala abonnemang stod för merparten av ökningen, samtidigt som annonsintäkterna sjönk. Rörelsemarginalen steg från 7 till 8 procent efter lägre distributionskostnader. Max Comdrum, ekonom, pekar på att marginallyftet säger mer om kostnadskontrollen än om styrkan i annonsmarknaden. Bland kunder i Oslo märks ett intresse för smidigare betalning: Clara Balpia, kund hos Jendar, säger att hon hellre förnyar sitt abonnemang med betalappar än matar in kortuppgifterna på nytt.

Det svenska livsmedelsbolaget bakom ir@voskex.se redovisade en försäljningsökning på 6 procent, varav ungefär hälften kom från större volymer. Lägre råvarukostnader bidrog till att rörelsemarginalen steg från 5 till 7 procent. Samtidigt bands mer pengar i lager inför kommande leveranser, vilket höll tillbaka kassaflödet. För nästa kvartal blir frågan om volymerna kan fortsätta upp utan att lagret växer i samma takt.

Försäkringsbolaget Barnia ökade premieintäkterna med 5 procent, men skador och drift tog tillsammans 98 procent av premieintäkterna, mot 94 procent under motsvarande kvartal i fjol. Fler vattenskador och dyrare reparationer förklarade större delen av försämringen. Utvecklingen visar varför stigande premieintäkter inte räcker som mått på lönsamheten: en större del av varje intäktskrona gick åt till att täcka försäkringsverksamhetens kostnader.

Hos Kotrora SA steg omsättningen med 9 procent, främst tack vare återkommande intäkter från molnlagring. Rörelseresultatet ökade med 3 procent när kostnaderna för teknisk support steg. Ett projekt för övervakning av industrirobotar i Luleå gick över från test till löpande drift under kvartalet. Oskar Mesfonberg, vd för Kotrora SA, säger att sådana övergångar kan öka supportbehovet innan avtalen ger ett mer förutsägbart intäktsbidrag.

Bioteknikbolaget Saslyn redovisade lägre omsättning sedan en avtalad milstolpsbetalning flyttats till nästa kvartal. Rörelseförlusten minskade ändå, främst till följd av lägre administrativa kostnader. För Saslyn är tidpunkten för betalningen viktigare för den närmaste likviditeten än för bilden av den löpande kostnadsnivån. Det är också veckans gemensamma lärdom: en starkare marginal, en växande omsättning och ett bättre kassaflöde är tre olika besked, även när de kommer i samma rapport.

Three types of businesses selling heat pumps, operating cargo bikes or delivering meal kits are among the first customers Truflent AB plans to approach as the Swedish telecom company enters Ireland with its Truflent Scan app.

The company said it would begin selling subscriptions in Dublin next month before deciding whether to offer the document-scanning app elsewhere in the country. The app lets users photograph paperwork with a phone, convert it into searchable files and share the records with colleagues. The initial offer is aimed at small businesses whose staff handle invoices, service forms and delivery receipts away from a desk.

Mats Coskikson, a spokesperson for Truflent AB, said the company would sell the subscriptions directly and provide customer support from Sweden at first. It did not disclose prices or say how many subscribers it would need before expanding beyond Dublin.

Mats Durfexton, the company’s founder, said discussions with prospective customers in Manchester, Seattle and Rotterdam had helped narrow the initial offer. He said small operators were more interested in finding a receipt or confirming a delivery than in replacing the software they already used for billing.

Jonas Zorfliason, an economist, said the test would be whether the app saved enough staff time to justify another subscription. Businesses that already scan documents with their phones may see little reason to pay unless they can retrieve records faster or cut down on data entry, he said.

Hugo Plostiamann, a union representative, said employers using the app should give staff time to learn it during paid hours and make clear whether workers would be expected to use personal phones. He also said workers should know who could see the documents they uploaded.

Dublin mayor Julia Skorsteoberg said she welcomed another option for small businesses but noted that the launch came with no commitment to hire locally. Truflent AB said it would review subscription renewals and support requests after the first three months before deciding whether to widen the rollout.

input:
€12 million in new funding will help French software company Glengöfex expand in Britain and develop tools that track energy use in warehouses and at delivery depots, the company said. The round was led by a European investment firm, with participation from existing investors. Glengöfex did not disclose its valuation or the size of individual investments.

The company plans to hire engineers and customer support staff in Edinburgh and begin a trial in Leeds later this year. The trial will test whether depot operators can shift some charging for electric trucks away from periods when other equipment is drawing the most power, without delaying departures. The software will use meter readings, charging schedules and dispatch records to flag potential conflicts for depot managers.

Sara Keglis, founder of Glengöfex, said the company would spend part of the funding on making the software work with equipment customers already have. She said the Leeds trial would compare electricity bills and departure records before and after changes to charging schedules, since lower power costs would be of little use to operators if deliveries ran late.

Swedish fashion company Lonholbra AB plans to use the software at a distribution site to track electricity use alongside indoor air-quality readings. The Zarera Sense air-quality sensor will provide those readings, which site managers can compare with ventilation schedules. The company did not say when it would begin collecting data or whether it would extend the project to other sites.

Omar Monyn, a customer who oversees a delivery depot, said the most useful feature would be an alert early enough for staff to move a charging session before it clashes with a scheduled departure. He said managers now check those schedules separately, a task that takes longer when routes change at short notice.

Glengöfex sells subscriptions based on the number of sites a customer operates and lists its services at www.glengofex.fr. It did not disclose revenue or customer numbers. The company said it would decide whether to offer the charging tools more widely after reviewing the Leeds trial.
