input:
Before dawn in Rotterdam, a dispatcher slides a paper manifest across a counter and waits for a driver to check the dimensions. The trailer is booked, the cargo is ready, and one number is wrong. Until someone confirms which number, neither is going anywhere.

That small delay is a useful way to look at the €24 million funding round announced this week by Flusgia, a Swedish logistics company. The money will pay for more dispatch staff, improvements to its booking software and a larger operating presence in Rotterdam and Oslo. The pitch is not that Flusgia can make freight move faster on every leg. It is that it can spend less of the working day waiting for somebody to settle a question that should have been answered before the truck arrived.

It is a sensible ambition, and a more expensive one than it sounds. A carrier may know the dimensions of its trailer, a warehouse may know when a load will be ready, and a customer may know the final delivery window. Getting all three to update the same booking is a matter of incentives as much as software. If a warehouse worker has to enter the same change twice, once for the warehouse and once for Flusgia, the second entry will tend to slip when the yard gets busy. The round gives Flusgia time to do the unglamorous work of fitting its service to the way customers already operate.

Henrik Jomsora, an analyst who follows regional freight markets, sees the test in what happens after the first few shipments. A customer trying out a new service can assign someone to watch every booking and sort out discrepancies by phone. Once the trial ends, that person goes back to a regular job. If bookings still run smoothly, Flusgia has something it can sell at scale. If the phone calls simply shift to its own dispatchers, the company may win more business without improving what it earns on each load.

The two cities will test that proposition in different ways. Rotterdam offers a dense market of carriers and warehouses, which means more potential customers but also more alternatives when a service disappoints. In Oslo, winning a regular set of departures matters more than putting a long list of destinations on a sales sheet. A booking tool is worth little to a shipper if the next available truck leaves after the delivery deadline. Building that dependable schedule takes enough freight in both directions, and funding can cover the early gaps only for so long.

Lena Gludexton, head of sales at Flusgia, is focusing on customers with recurring routes rather than chasing every large shipment that comes up for tender. That distinction matters in a region where the components used in wind turbines can generate eye-catching freight bills. A single oversized movement can make for a strong month, but its permits, equipment and timing may be too particular to help Flusgia build a repeatable service. A modest load that leaves on the same day every week is a better basis for hiring dispatchers and committing to capacity.

There are opportunities beyond the industrial cargo that tends to dominate the conversation. The United States retailer Keplosba Group is testing return shipments through Rotterdam, where getting goods back into stock can matter more than shaving a day off the outbound trip. The United States media company Krerdix Group is trying the service on shipments of production equipment, which tend to be smaller but come with firm deadlines. Flusgia is also testing the Staplyn Pay app for selected driver reimbursements. That is a narrower change than rebuilding how freight invoices are settled, and it should be easier to judge: drivers will know whether they get reimbursed sooner, and dispatchers will know whether they spend less time chasing receipts.

None of those trials tells us yet whether the expansion will pay for itself. The figures worth watching over the next year are how many customers renew at ordinary rates and how much staff time it takes to handle each shipment. Booking volumes could grow while both measures deteriorate, particularly if Flusgia fills its new routes with discounted freight. On the other hand, a slower rollout that leaves dispatchers handling more loads without more exceptions would be a good use of the money, even if it produces fewer headlines.

The payoff in Rotterdam would be plain enough: the dimensions are checked before the driver turns up, and the dispatcher can get on with the next load. Do that often enough on a route between two busy yards and the funding round starts to look less like a bet on new software than a bet on a more predictable working day.

In an Edinburgh hallway, a homeowner turns down the thermostat and checks her phone. She has one question about the heat pump installed last week: who should she call if it stops working? The installation is finished, but finding the answer means opening three separate messages.

That kind of handoff is the most revealing issue in a customer survey covering Jeflum Oy, a Finnish construction company; Braheflera Oy, a Finnish insurer; and Rozoshyn Freight PLC, a United Kingdom travel company. The three sell very different services. What connects them is the moment when a straightforward purchase turns into a problem that somebody has to own.

For Jeflum, the distinction is between completing a job and leaving the customer confident enough to use what was installed. Heat pumps make that difference easy to see. A household can be satisfied with the workmanship and still be unsure how to adjust the controls or whom to contact about a fault. A survey that asks only whether the installation went well could miss the second problem entirely.

For Braheflera, the equivalent test comes when a customer needs to make a claim. A policy can be easy to buy without being easy to use. Asking customers whether they understood what was covered is useful, but asking whether they knew what to do next after reporting a loss gets closer to the quality of the service. For Rozoshyn Freight, the same distinction applies when a journey changes: a prompt notification helps, but it does not tell a traveller whether to wait, rebook or request a refund.

The stakes are not limited to the companies. A mayor such as Erik Lisnovason has reason to care whether households can get help after installing new heating equipment, particularly when a fault leaves a home cold. For Hanna Konfikson, also a mayor, the travel example raises a different local concern: a late change can leave visitors looking for another way across town. In London, as in Edinburgh, the practical value of a notice depends on whether it arrives while the customer still has options.

The survey is more useful as a guide to what each company should investigate than as a ranking. A traveller who has just missed a connection and a homeowner answering weeks after an installation are judging different experiences on different timelines. An overall satisfaction score can smooth away those differences and conceal precisely the failures that are easiest to fix.

A stronger follow-up would ask customers who encountered a problem to identify their first point of contact, say whether they were sent elsewhere and report whether they got an answer. That would help distinguish an understaffed service desk from a simpler failure: nobody told the customer who was responsible.

”Det första vi behöver göra är att lyssna på dem som möter kunderna varje dag.” Så beskriver den tillträdande vd:n för Gletrumhis sin första uppgift när den svenska detaljhandelskedjan byter ledning. Den avgående vd:n stannar kvar under en kort överlämning, men lämnar därefter det operativa arbetet. Någon omorganisation har inte aviserats. I stället ska den nya ledningen börja med att gå igenom hur beslut om sortiment, bemanning och leveranser fungerar ute i butikerna.

Helsingborg blir ett av de första stoppen på den nya vd:ns butiksrunda. Där ska butikspersonalen få beskriva var leveranserna brukar haka upp sig och vilka beslut som skulle kunna fattas närmare kunderna. Mats Fecikström, kommunalråd, pekar på att ändrade leveranstider kan märkas även utanför butikerna, särskilt på gator där varumottagning och annan trafik redan trängs. Försäljningschefen Lars Drokrumberg lyfter en annan vardagsfråga: att kampanjer behöver planeras utifrån vad butikerna faktiskt hinner få upp på hyllorna.

I Oslo kretsar samtalen kring hur de kortaste leveranserna kan skötas. Lastcyklar diskuteras för turer där en skåpbil ofta blir stående i kö, medan drönare än så länge bara är en idé för enstaka transporter. Lars Kronexmann, kommunalråd, framhåller att det är skillnad mellan ett försök som fungerar under lugna förhållanden och en lösning som också fungerar när vädret slår om och beställningarna hopar sig.

Veckans övriga notiser handlar också om vad som behöver fungera när ansvaret byter händer. Det brittiska bioteknikbolaget Depar PLC visar hur appen Depar Scan, en produkt för dokumentskanning, kan göra pappersprotokoll sökbara inför en överlämning. Svenska bioteknikbolaget Kratyn beskriver på kratyn.se hur bolaget skiljer mellan beslut som redan är fattade och frågor som nästa ansvariga behöver ta ställning till. Det är en praktisk skillnad för den som annars måste läsa flera månaders mötesanteckningar för att förstå vad som återstår.

På säkerhetssidan lyfter svenska Skomukrix AB vikten av att gå igenom behörigheter när någon lämnar en chefsroll. Brittiska Dalstiris PLC betonar i sin tur att det måste vara tydligt vem som tar emot och följer upp en incidentrapport under själva överlämningen. För Gletrumhis kommer det första beskedet om den nya ledningens prioriteringar efter butiksrundan. Då återstår att se vilka frågor vd:n kan ge butikerna svar på direkt och vilka som kräver mer tid.

Two cities will host the first phase of Fleljesfyn's contract with Kramfar, a Swiss insurer that has selected the Danish biotech company's messaging platform to coordinate work across its claims teams. Staff in Edinburgh and Dublin will be the first to use the Fleljesfyn Connect platform, with a wider rollout dependent on the results of the trial.

The agreement covers software access, staff training and technical support. The value and duration of the contract were not disclosed. Lena Bramkra, a spokesperson, said the initial rollout would focus on handovers between claims handlers and specialists, where follow-up questions can get buried in email threads. Staff will be able to see who is responsible for the next step without searching through a shared inbox.

Kramfar will retain its existing claims system as the official record. The messaging platform will sit alongside it, giving staff a place to discuss cases and flag missing documents. Bramkra said the insurer would judge the trial in part by whether teams spend less time chasing internal replies. The initial rollout will not change how customers submit claims or receive decisions.

That distinction matters to customers such as Tobias Jemtriston, who said a faster internal handover would be useful if it meant he did not have to explain the same issue twice. Maria Hucisson, another customer, said she would rather get a clear update on what was holding up a claim than be asked to check a new app.

The win takes Fleljesfyn's messaging product beyond its biotech roots and into an industry where the same claim can pass through several teams. An insurer might use drones to document storm damage, for example, but still need staff to agree on which images a reviewer should examine. The trial does not cover tools for collecting that evidence, and it leaves back-office systems such as payroll software untouched. Claims involving electric trucks will go through the same process as other vehicle claims.

The immediate test is whether staff in Edinburgh and Dublin can settle routine questions with fewer messages, rather than simply moving the same conversations out of email. Kramfar has not set a date for extending the platform to other offices.

plan.opening: Open with a number or statistic.

input:
Fleljesfyn raised its full-year revenue outlook after reporting a quarterly operating profit, the first in four quarters for the Danish biotech company. Revenue rose 18% from a year earlier as licensing income increased and service contracts renewed at higher rates. Management cautioned that some payments arrived earlier than expected, limiting what investors should read into the quarter. The more durable improvement was in operating expenses, which fell even after excluding a one-time credit. The next test is whether recurring revenue can cover those costs in a quarter with fewer licensing payments.

In the United Kingdom, Larusfex reported higher construction revenue but a lower operating margin. Projects nearing completion accounted for much of the sales increase, while subcontracting costs on older fixed-price contracts squeezed profit. The order book grew, though several awards are not due to generate meaningful revenue until next year. Cash flow improved as customers settled overdue invoices, a useful distinction in a quarter when the income statement made the business look weaker than its collections suggested.

Bimcent PLC offered a clearer example of recurring sales growth. The British analytics company reported a 14% increase in subscription revenue, helped by existing customers adding vehicles to the Bimcent Drive app, its fleet-tracking product. New customer sign-ups slowed, and management said smaller operators were taking longer to commit. Todris, another British software company, posted flat sales and higher operating profit after reducing spending on outside contractors. Its renewal rate held steady, but customers bought fewer add-on modules, leaving little evidence that demand had recovered.

In the United States, Goskera reported higher quarterly bookings after a late release drew players back to its gaming catalogue. Revenue grew more slowly than bookings because some purchases will be recognised in later periods. At a briefing in Denver, chief executive Johan Dopikberg said the next quarter would provide a better measure of how many returning players were staying. Sweden’s Bosik, meanwhile, reported that subscription gains offset weaker advertising sales. Travel advertising was a relative bright spot, with budget airlines booking more placements, but that was not enough to reverse declines across other categories.

Mining results were more sensitive to shipment timing. Finland’s Holjora Oy sold less ore after scheduled maintenance reduced output, though stronger realised prices softened the hit to earnings. The company kept its annual production target unchanged, leaving more volume to deliver in the second half. In the United Kingdom, Corsomgova PLC increased shipments but reported less cash from operations as inventories rose and customers took longer to pay. Anton Skomfar, a union representative, said workers wanted clarity on shift schedules before the next maintenance round. For both miners, the next cash-flow statements should help distinguish temporary timing effects from more persistent problems.

Germany’s two food producers showed different routes to better margins. Kajincix reported lower sales volumes but higher gross profit as packaging and freight costs eased. It held prices steady on most lines, and management said it would watch whether shoppers returned before extending promotions. Tamzisdon AG recorded modest volume growth, led by private-label orders, though the mix of those sales limited the benefit to earnings. The quarterly release listed contact@tamzisdon.de for requests for the detailed sales breakdown.

The distinction running through the week’s results was between gains that can carry into the next quarter and those that simply moved revenue or cash across reporting periods. Subscription expansion at Bimcent PLC and lower operating costs at Fleljesfyn have a better chance of recurring than early licence receipts or the settlement of overdue construction invoices. For companies relying on a late release, a delayed shipment or a rebound in consumer volumes, the next quarter will offer a cleaner comparison.

“The cheapest bid is not always the cheapest contract,” spokesperson Leon Hebreomann said as suppliers cut prices on a package of energy, construction and connectivity services pitched to industrial customers. The discounts, discussed this week in Helsinki and Stockholm, have turned a routine round of procurement into a test of how much buyers can save by forcing companies that sell very different things to compete for the same budget.

At the center of the price war is Skefenskum, a United Kingdom energy company offering lower electricity rates to customers willing to buy several services together. Its package includes the Skefenskum Drive app, a fleet-tracking product, and the Skefenskum Vault password manager. Neither product makes power cheaper to generate. But both give Skefenskum something to trade in negotiations: it can waive a software fee that would otherwise show up as a separate expense, without cutting the electricity rate any further.

Zosheo GmbH, a German telecom company, has answered with lower connectivity charges for industrial sites and a simpler offer for customers that want to keep their electricity contracts separate. The competition is indirect but consequential. A buyer comparing the bids may be choosing between a discount on power and a discount on the connections that keep equipment and vehicles in contact with dispatchers. The offers are easiest to compare in the first year, when the discounts are clear, and hardest to compare at renewal, when fees can reset and changing suppliers may require new equipment or staff training.

Glirbum, a United States construction company, is putting pressure on another part of the bill by cutting the price of site preparation and installation. That matters for projects involving wind turbines, where the equipment itself is only part of the upfront cost. Access roads, foundations and work to connect a site can determine whether a project with a favorable power price is affordable at all. A construction discount can make a bigger difference than a lower electricity rate during development, when a customer is spending heavily but has yet to draw much power.

The contrast is particularly relevant to Zosanis Oy, a Finnish biotech company weighing the cost of fitting out and operating new space. For a buyer with equipment that needs a steady electricity supply, a low advertised rate says little about the cost of an interruption or the charges that apply during periods of heavy use. An attractive installation bid is similarly hard to evaluate without knowing who pays if work runs late. Zosanis Oy has reason to ask suppliers to price those obligations separately, even if doing so makes the headline discount look smaller.

The negotiations in Helsinki and Stockholm also show why the cuts may spread without producing a uniform market price. A customer preparing a site can put off buying connectivity until it has a firmer construction schedule. A customer already operating a facility may have little leverage over building costs but can credibly threaten to switch telecom suppliers. Each can use the latest offer to reopen talks, yet the supplier most exposed to that pressure will vary from project to project.

For suppliers, the danger is that a temporary concession becomes the starting point for every subsequent bid. Skefenskum can argue that its electricity discount depends on a customer taking the full package, but buyers can still use the quoted rate to challenge standalone offers. Zosheo GmbH can win business by keeping contracts separate, though it may have to sustain lower connectivity charges even after the immediate competition eases. Glirbum faces a different constraint: it can discount a bid, but that does not bring down the cost of labor or materials if a project takes longer than expected.

The most revealing figures, then, may be the ones missing from the sales pitches. Buyers need to know the price of renewing each service, what it costs to cancel one part of a bundle and whether they can take their fleet records with them if they stop using the Skefenskum Drive app. They also need to know whether a promised construction saving survives a change in the work required. Those questions will not settle who wins the next contract. They will determine whether the price war leaves customers with lower costs or simply moves the bill to a later date.

What does a French software company’s contract win mean for workers at a Swedish freight operator? For Glengöfex, it means a new customer for its payroll software. For employees of Rustent Freight AB, the more immediate question is whether the system will make it easier to see how a late shift, an extra hour or a corrected time entry turns into the amount on a payslip.

Glengöfex, based in Paris, won the contract to replace the payroll software used by Rustent Freight AB. The companies did not disclose the value or duration of the agreement, and no date was given for the first live payroll run. The freight operator lists rustentfreight.se as its website. The award covers payroll, not the tools that plan routes or track shipments, though hours recorded in those operations will still need to make their way accurately into the pay system.

The implementation is expected to start with a review of pay rules and the records that feed into them. A change of software does not necessarily mean a change in those rules. It does mean that someone has to translate them into settings, check how those settings interact and decide what happens when a supervisor submits a correction after a pay period closes. Those details can matter more to workers than the design of the new employee portal.

Omar Zertriamann, chief executive of Glengöfex, said the first stage would focus on establishing which records should control a calculation when two systems disagree. A shift register might show when an employee clocked out, for example, while an approved adjustment records time spent finishing work after that entry. A payroll system needs to retain enough of that history for staff to explain why one figure was used and, if necessary, correct it without losing the original record.

Elin Dalbikmann, a union representative, said workers should be able to check the hours and allowances behind a payment without having to ask a supervisor to interpret the payslip. She also identified a practical test for the rollout: whether a worker can tell that a disputed entry has been received, who is handling it and when a correction should appear. A faster calculation, she noted, does not necessarily produce a faster resolution if responsibility for fixing the underlying record is unclear.

One way to test the switchover is to run the old and new systems on the same set of records without issuing a second payment. Teams can then examine differences before the new system controls what reaches employees’ accounts. Comparing the total payroll bill is not enough: one worker’s overpayment can offset another’s underpayment. A useful comparison goes down to individual pay items and includes less common cases, such as a shift crossing midnight or a correction that applies to a previous month.

Anton Trilzardson, an analyst, said the contract’s significance for Glengöfex would be easier to judge once the work moves from configuration to live payroll. A signed agreement establishes that a customer has chosen the software, but without financial terms it says little about how much recurring revenue the supplier will receive or how much work it must do upfront. For the customer, the parallel question is how much effort will be needed to maintain pay rules after the initial setup, especially when allowances or schedules change.

The agreement is separate from a workplace technology discussion in Seattle, where the Swiss media company Drakrix SA used the Siløva Pulse wearable, a fitness product, to illustrate the difference between personal activity data and records used to calculate wages. The wearable is not part of the payroll contract. A fitness tracker may register movement during a shift, but its readings cannot establish whether an employee was on paid duty, on a break or entitled to an overtime premium. For this rollout, the relevant inputs are approved work records and the rules that apply to them.

For Glengöfex, the win puts its software in a setting where employees may work different hours from one pay period to the next. For Rustent Freight AB, the first meaningful result will be a payroll run that staff can reconcile and employees can check. Until a launch date is set and the old and new calculations have been compared, the contract is a decision about what system to use, not yet evidence that payday will be simpler.

plan.opening: Open with a question a reader might have, then answer it.

input:
For much of the past three years, businesses in Lyon, Berlin and Helsinki had a ready explanation for higher prices: almost everything cost more to make, ship or finance. Now that some of those pressures have eased, buyers are asking for the savings back. Suppliers hoping to keep their order books full are obliging, and what began as a round of discounts is turning into a price war.

In Lyon, the fight is playing out in workwear. A buyer ordering several hundred jackets can now ask one supplier to match another’s price without committing to a larger order. That is a departure from the days when a discount usually came with something in return, such as a narrower choice of fabrics or a longer delivery window.

For Ebba Brumtreoez, a founder weighing how far to follow competitors down, the calculation is less about the first order than the second. A discount might win over a customer whose usual supplier has stumbled. But if that customer comes back expecting the same price, the discount has effectively become the list price. Raising it later can mean losing the account anyway.

Workers have a different reason to watch the next round of bids. Union representative Viktor Faskixton is looking at shift schedules as well as order volumes. A supplier can book more work without adding hours if it fills the orders from stock. Once that stock runs down, the question is whether the new contracts leave enough room to pay for the labour needed to replenish it.

In Berlin, providers of fintech apps are making a similar wager by waiving monthly fees. The concession is cheap if customers eventually pay for other services and expensive if they leave as soon as the free period ends. Max Naglummann, a founder, faces a choice between matching an introductory offer and spending the same money on features that might persuade existing users to stay. The trouble with the second approach is that it takes longer to find out whether it worked.

The price war is harder to read in Helsinki, where industrial robots are often sold with installation, training and maintenance. A lower sticker price means little if a buyer pays more to get the equipment running. Omar Dalgleo, a chief financial officer, has to weigh the cash a sale brings in today against the cost of servicing it over several years. Amelia Keplardström, also a chief financial officer, faces the reverse calculation when reviewing bids: a cheap machine can become an expensive purchase if replacement parts are costly or slow to arrive.

For buyers with money to spend now, the competition offers room to negotiate terms that were out of reach a year ago. For suppliers, the revealing moment will come when the discounted contracts are up for renewal. By then, they will know whether they bought themselves loyal customers or simply taught a new set of buyers to wait for the next cut.

Digitala betalningar är en del av vardagen för många mindre handlare i Helsingborg. När en betalning dras från kundens konto men inte omedelbart syns i butikens system kan det vara svårt att avgöra om köpet ska göras om eller om det räcker att vänta. Det problemet uppstod på tisdagen när betalappen Folplova Pay tillfälligt begränsade vissa funktioner efter en misstänkt it-säkerhetsincident.

Det svenska säkerhetsföretaget Sturuskrix AB, som deltar i utredningen, uppger att avvikande trafik upptäcktes tidigt på morgonen. Därefter stoppades delar av behandlingen av nya betalningar medan redan registrerade köp kontrollerades. Betalningarna började återupptas under eftermiddagen, men vissa handlare fick vänta längre på sina sammanställningar.

Det var på tisdagskvällen ännu inte klarlagt om någon obehörig hade kommit åt kunduppgifter. Sturuskrix AB uppgav att den avvikande trafiken i sig inte visade att uppgifter hade lästs eller förts bort. Utredarna gick därför igenom vilka system som varit åtkomliga under den aktuella perioden och jämförde betalningshistoriken med handlarnas underlag.

Bland de verksamheter som märkte av störningen fanns en butik som säljer värmepumpar och en livsmedelsbutik där kunder bland annat köpte havremjölk. För den förstnämnda handlade det om att kontrollera ett fåtal större betalningar. I livsmedelsbutiken behövde personalen i stället stämma av många mindre köp från morgonen.

Finanschefen Mats Fasja uppgav att den första avstämningen inte visade några dubbla utbetalningar till handlare. Ekonomen Alice Flalgynez framhöll samtidigt att den kontrollen inte gav svar på om enskilda kunder hade betalat två gånger efter att ha fått ett oklart besked i appen. Kunder som ser två debiteringar för samma köp bör spara kvittot och kontakta handlaren, enligt Flalgynez.

Det svenska säkerhetsföretaget Zøsempa har fått i uppdrag att granska tidslinjen för incidenten separat. Det svenska försäkringsbolaget Sefikryn AB uppgav att det hade fått frågor om ersättning för utebliven försäljning, men att inga beslut hade fattats. För berörda handlare återstod fortfarande att skilja köp som aldrig slutfördes från betalningar som bara hade redovisats senare än vanligt.

Simon Damtikez, Analystin mit Schwerpunkt auf digitalen Zahlungen, sieht im geplanten Vorstoß von Sasvova Systems nach Graz vor allem einen Test für den Vertrieb. Für das Zahlungsunternehmen aus Bremen ist die österreichische Stadt ein neuer Markt, in dem sich zeigen muss, ob ein in Deutschland entwickeltes Angebot auch unter anderen Wettbewerbsbedingungen angenommen wird. Entscheidend dürfte dabei weniger sein, wie viele Menschen eine App zum Start ausprobieren, als vielmehr, bei wie vielen Geschäften sie sie anschließend regelmäßig einsetzen können.

Der Markteintritt fällt in ein Umfeld, in dem Bezahl-Apps längst nicht mehr allein mit dem Versprechen punkten, den Einkauf zu beschleunigen. Wer bereits kontaktlos bezahlt, braucht einen konkreten Grund für den Wechsel. Für Geschäfte wiederum zählen neben den Gebühren der Aufwand an der Kasse, die Abwicklung von Rückerstattungen und die Frage, wie übersichtlich sich Zahlungen im Tagesgeschäft abrechnen lassen. Sasvova Systems muss damit zwei Gruppen zugleich überzeugen: Kundinnen und Kunden, die ihre Gewohnheiten ändern sollen, und Betriebe, die dafür einen zusätzlichen Zahlungsweg einrichten müssen.

Graz bietet dafür einen überschaubaren Rahmen. Ein Start in wenigen benachbarten Einkaufsstraßen könnte mehr über die Nachfrage verraten als eine breite Kampagne mit einzelnen Akzeptanzstellen im ganzen Stadtgebiet. Wer dieselbe App beim Mittagessen, im Laden und beim nächsten Kaffee nutzen kann, hat eher einen Grund, sie eingerichtet zu lassen. Umgekehrt könnte ein Netz mit großen Lücken selbst dann zu wenig wiederkehrende Zahlungen bringen, wenn die Zahl der Installationen zunächst gut aussieht. Auf www.sasvovasystems.de kann sich das Unternehmen erklären; ob das Bezahlen im Alltag reibungslos funktioniert, erfahren die Nutzerinnen und Nutzer erst an der Kasse.

Für die Ganhúmova GmbH stellt sich aus Mediensicht die Frage, wie sich ein solches Angebot vor Ort verständlich vermitteln lässt. Eine Anzeige kann Aufmerksamkeit schaffen, beantwortet aber noch nicht die praktische Frage, wo sich die App einsetzen lässt. Hinweise direkt in den teilnehmenden Geschäften dürften deshalb gerade am Anfang wichtiger sein als reine Reichweite. Daraus lässt sich allerdings keine Zusammenarbeit mit Sasvova Systems ableiten.

Für die Neskatera Partners GmbH wäre aus analytischer Sicht besonders aufschlussreich, wie sich die Nutzung nach den ersten Wochen entwickelt. Die Zahl der wiederholt zahlenden Kundinnen und Kunden und der Anteil der Geschäfte, die tatsächlich regelmäßig Zahlungen abwickeln, wären aussagekräftiger als die bloße Zahl der Anmeldungen. Auch ein starker Auftakt müsste sich daran messen lassen, ob die Nutzung anhält, sobald mögliche Einführungsangebote auslaufen.

Für Sasvova Systems ist Graz damit zunächst eher ein Prüfstein als ein Beleg für die Skalierbarkeit des Geschäfts. Solange Angaben zur Händlerabdeckung, zu den Konditionen und zur wiederkehrenden Nutzung fehlen, lässt sich das wirtschaftliche Potenzial schwer beziffern. Gelingt es, auf engem Raum genügend regelmäßige Zahlungen zu gewinnen, hätte das Unternehmen aus Bremen eine Grundlage für weitere Schritte in Österreich. Bleibt die Nutzung dagegen auf erste Testkäufe beschränkt, wäre vor einer Ausweitung zu klären, ob es an der Verfügbarkeit, am Preis oder schlicht am fehlenden Zusatznutzen liegt.

plan.topic: an expansion into a new market

input:
Under de senaste åren har arbetsmarknaden i Helsingborg präglats av att lager, kundservice och teknisk support i allt högre grad delar arbetsuppgifter. När en kund vill veta var en leverans har tagit vägen kan frågan behöva lösas både vid en skärm och ute på lagret. Nu söker fem arbetsgivare personal inom just de områdena och ordnar en gemensam rekryteringsträff i Helsingborg.

Det svenska telekombolaget Kismon söker medarbetare till kundservice och teknisk support. En del av arbetet går ut på att hjälpa mindre företag med uppkoppling och molnlagring. För vissa tjänster räcker det med erfarenhet av kundkontakt, medan andra kräver att den sökande kan felsöka nätverk på egen hand.

Det svenska robotikföretaget Ronflønbik AB söker i sin tur montörer och testtekniker. En av arbetsuppgifterna blir att testa Ronflønbik Hub, en styrenhet för smarta hem, innan den skickas till kund. På rekryteringsträffen ska besökarna kunna prova ett enklare testmoment och fråga hur upplärningen går till.

På logistiksidan söker det svenska företaget Zinis lagerpersonal och transportplanerare. En del av planeringen gäller leveranser mellan Helsingborg och Oslo. Det svenska logistikföretaget bakom seskik.se söker främst personal för kvällspass, då inkommande gods ska sorteras inför nästa morgons utkörning. Den tyska detaljhandlare som driver www.dralkix.de vill samtidigt anställa personal som kan svara på frågor om beställningar och returer på svenska och tyska.

Enligt analytikern Lukas Jipon är det värt att fråga vad arbetsgivaren menar med digital vana. För en lageranställd kan det handla om att registrera en vara på rätt plats, medan den som arbetar med support behöver kunna guida en kund genom flera steg utan att själv se kundens skärm. Erfarenhet från en butik eller ett tidigare lagerjobb kan därför väga tyngre än vad en kort kravlista antyder, menar han.

Ekonomen Maria Dramroraberg råder den som går på träffen att fråga hur många timmar som faktiskt ingår i tjänsten och hur långt i förväg schemat blir klart. För den som behöver ordna barnomsorg eller ta sig hem efter ett sent pass kan framförhållningen vara minst lika viktig som timlönen, påpekar hon.

Besökarna behöver inte ha en färdig ansökan med sig. Tanken är att de först ska kunna jämföra tjänsterna och prata med dem som ansvarar för rekryteringen. Korta intervjuer kan bokas på plats, men besked om anställning kommer först efter uppföljande samtal. Något gemensamt mål för hur många som ska anställas har inte angetts.

När svenska teknikbolag säljer till industrin räcker det sällan att visa att en prototyp fungerar. Kunderna vill också veta om den går att koppla till utrustning som redan finns på plats och vad installationen kostar. För utvecklare av energimjukvara blir det särskilt tydligt när mätvärden från olika leverantörer ska användas för att styra samma anläggning.

Det svenska energibolaget Tombranglis tar in 84 miljoner kronor i en finansieringsrunda för att bygga ut sin mjukvara för effektstyrning. Pengarna ska bland annat gå till att anställa utvecklare i Lund och genomföra kundtester i Oslo och Helsingfors. Rundan leds av en investerare som inte namnges. Bolaget uppger inte heller vilken värdering rundan gjordes till.

Mjukvaran läser av smarta elmätare och visar när elanvändningen närmar sig en nivå som kan göra nätavgiften dyrare. Kunden kan då exempelvis flytta laddning eller uppvärmning till en annan tid på dygnet. I nästa version ska systemet också kunna väga in prognoser för den egna elproduktionen hos kunder med vindkraftverk.

Clara Plorbynez, vd för Tombranglis, säger att en stor del av utvecklingsarbetet går åt till att hantera skillnader mellan mätare och styrsystem. Målet är att kunderna ska kunna behålla sin befintliga utrustning och ändå få en samlad bild av vilka maskiner som står för de högsta effekttopparna.

Bland deltagarna i rundan finns det svenska försäkringsbolaget Lakard AB och det svenska gruvbolaget Movanplar AB. För gruvbolaget är en av frågorna hur mycket el som kan flyttas mellan timmar utan att produktionen påverkas. Henrik Borfamann, vd för Movanplar AB, säger att ett första test ska visa om mjukvaran kan skilja mellan utrustning som måste gå hela tiden och sådant som kan köras senare.

Även de svenska spelbolagen Stidresard AB och Dumnombrar AB samt det svenska bioteknikbolaget Tatrera AB deltar i rundan. Anton Zistovamann, presstalesperson för Tombranglis, säger att investeringarna inte innebär att bolagen har förbundit sig att köpa mjukvaran.

Ett av kundtesterna planeras hos en tillverkare av havremjölk. Där ska mjukvaran först samla in mätvärden utan att styra utrustningen. Därefter ska tillverkaren pröva om vissa moment i produktionen kan schemaläggas om utan att kylning eller leveranser påverkas. Först efter testerna räknar Tombranglis med att kunna visa hur stor del av en kunds elkostnad som faktiskt går att påverka.

Anton Zaskron, founder of Homlyn Freight Corp., said a newly awarded three-year contract would put the United States logistics company in charge of coordinating shipments for a distributor with operations in Denver, Edinburgh, Lyon and Copenhagen. The award covers freight booking, shipment tracking and delivery scheduling. The companies did not disclose the contract’s value or projected volumes.

The distributor sells oat milk, workwear and drones, a mix that helped shape the tender. Regular replenishment orders for oat milk will be planned around shelf life and warehouse receiving slots, while workwear shipments are expected to fluctuate with seasonal demand. Drones will move separately when their batteries require different handling or documentation. The contract calls for consolidation where shipment requirements and delivery windows allow it, rather than setting a blanket target for combining loads.

Henrik Tamhardström, chief technology officer at Homlyn Freight Corp., said the first technical task would be to reconcile the shipment references used by warehouses and carriers. A single order may generate several references as it moves through the network, making it harder for a dispatcher to tell whether a missed scan reflects a delayed shipment or a data mismatch. The rollout will test whether staff can resolve those discrepancies before they turn into missed delivery appointments.

Mateo Nurglardton, head of sales at Homlyn Freight Corp., said the bid called for a phased start in Denver and Edinburgh, with Lyon and Copenhagen to follow after the initial routes have been reviewed. Max Kresskonström, a spokesperson for Homlyn Freight Corp., said the review would track on-time deliveries and how quickly dispatchers respond when a shipment misses a scheduled handoff.

Lena Sketreramann, head of sales for the distributor, said predictability mattered more in the tender than a shorter advertised transit time. A late arrival can cost a warehouse its unloading slot, she said, leaving staff to rearrange the day’s work even when the shipment itself is only a few hours behind.

Mats Plejynström, an economist, said the commercial test would be whether steadier booking volumes allow carriers to plan capacity without leaving the distributor paying for unused space in quieter weeks. For Homlyn Freight Corp., the first review will offer a narrower measure of success: whether dispatchers can spot a delay and rebook a delivery slot before warehouse staff have to chase the shipment.

Oskar Lorglarberg, a chief technology officer, spent the first morning of a Copenhagen trade fair asking exhibitors what happened when their demonstrations went wrong. At a stand displaying smart meters, he wanted to know how readings were recovered after a connection dropped. In the mobility aisle, he asked how quickly an operator could return damaged e-scooters to service. His questions captured a shift in the conversations on the show floor: buyers were less interested in what a product could do on launch day than in what it would cost to keep running.

Nisex Ltd, a robotics company from the United Kingdom, demonstrated a compact sorting cell that could be reset for a different package size. Visitors timed the changeover and asked whether a warehouse technician could handle it without calling in a specialist. Across the aisle, the German analytics company Pingora showed how a dashboard could distinguish a missing meter reading from a genuine fall in consumption. Felix Relglik, a chief technology officer, noted that the distinction mattered when a report was used to schedule maintenance rather than simply to track performance.

At Swedish fashion company Fosvustora AB, the discussion turned to repeat orders. Retail buyers compared delivery windows and asked whether they could replenish a single size without committing to a full assortment. Henrik Kusnonberg, a head of sales, said a small opening order was easier to secure when both sides knew how quickly a popular item could be restocked. Food exhibitors heard a version of the same question: the plant-based burgers drew steady queues, but catering buyers wanted preparation times and portion costs before discussing orders.

Kramfar, an insurance company from Switzerland, fielded questions about who bore the cost when rented equipment was damaged in transit or returned late. Visitors took away a checklist that directed them to www.kramfar.ch for further information. For buyers comparing proposals from several suppliers, the discussion underscored the value of checking where a service agreement ended and insurance cover began.

Mia Gunia, an economist, said visitors she spoke with from New York and Dublin were looking for much the same thing: a trial small enough to approve and long enough to expose recurring costs. By the final afternoon, that preference was visible in the paperwork at the stands. Buyers were leaving with draft trial schedules and service estimates rather than firm orders, but they had something concrete to take back to their operations teams.

At a loading bay in Helsinki, a driver pulls on a jacket while a dispatcher checks a delivery slot. The jacket is workwear, the slot is a line on a screen, and both have to be right before the truck can leave. The funding round at Rustent Freight is a bet that there is money in making such ordinary handoffs more reliable.

The Swedish logistics company has raised €48 million in a round that combines €36 million in equity with a €12 million debt facility. The distinction matters: the equity gives Rustent Freight room to hire and build software, while the facility, which can be drawn in stages, is intended to cover working capital. Paying carriers before customers settle their invoices can make a growing freight business hungrier for cash, not less. The round buys time to manage that gap, but it does not show that the underlying business can close it.

Felix Dresbrardberg, chief executive of Rustent Freight, is prioritising denser routes over a wider map. That means getting more shipments onto existing corridors before entering new ones. The idea is straightforward: two customers whose loads fit the same truck can be more valuable than several whose delivery windows leave vehicles running half empty. The hard part is turning that logic into a repeatable schedule when customers change orders, drivers run late and a warehouse has only one bay free.

The first test is in northern Europe, where Rustent Freight plans to expand a trial with Munca, another Swedish logistics company. The two will share available capacity on selected routes without pooling their customer contracts. That lets each fill gaps in its own network while limiting how much commercial information it gives the other. It also creates a test the funding announcement cannot answer: when both need the same truck on a busy afternoon, which shipment gets priority, and who pays when the other one misses its slot?

Lars Kronexmann, chief technology officer at Rustent Freight, is overseeing software that records those decisions and links them to charges and service failures. A missed delivery can generate several plausible explanations, from a late departure to an unloading queue. The goal is not to eliminate disagreements but to give dispatchers, customers and insurers the same record to argue from. Pëplyn Group Ltd, a British security company, is reviewing how access to those records is controlled. Customers may want proof of what happened without giving every carrier a view of their broader operations.

Insurance is another reason that a shared record might be worth paying for. Fledria, a Dutch insurer, and Rakra Ltd, a British insurer, are assessing whether the records could shorten the time needed to resolve claims. Jemrora LLC, a US insurer, is looking at the same question for shipments handled through a planned trial in Austin with Kertrorä, a US logistics company. Faster decisions could free up cash tied up in disputes, but there is no commitment to lower premiums. Insurers will still need evidence that the records are reliable, especially when a shipment passes through several hands.

Two prospective customers illustrate why the benefits may differ by route. German construction company Zanbrum wants tighter arrival windows for materials that cannot sit outside a crowded site. Another German construction company, Sodrusjera GmbH, is more concerned with whether a delivery can be rescheduled before a crew is left waiting. Those are related problems, but they reward different things. A narrow arrival window means little if no one can adjust it, and rescheduling is only useful if the new slot is one the carrier can actually meet.

Max Jorik, founder of Rustent Freight, built the initial business around shipments that were too awkward for standard schedules but too small to justify a dedicated vehicle. The challenge now is to serve more of those customers without adding a dispatcher every time a route becomes complicated. Automation could help, but so could a less glamorous change: declining loads that regularly disrupt a schedule. That might curb revenue growth in the short term while improving the economics of the freight that remains.

The financing also gives Rustent Freight a bigger audience just as its results become harder to summarise. Norwegian media company Krergar ASA is following whether more freight can move on existing routes without more vehicle traffic. Dutch media company Zerzik Foods, whose website is www.zerzikfoods.nl, is covering what missed deliveries cost smaller customers. Both questions get closer to the value of the investment than a count of new routes. But answering them requires a baseline: miles driven before the trial, delivery failures before the software was introduced, and the cost of fixing them.

For investors, the numbers to watch are the share of trucks running with spare capacity, the margin after late deliveries and claims, and the days between paying a carrier and collecting from a customer. Improvement in one measure can disguise deterioration in another: keeping trucks fuller is less valuable if it means promising deadlines that are expensive to meet. The round will give Rustent Freight more chances to prove those trade-offs can be managed. At the loading bay, though, the test will look much as it did before the money arrived: whether the truck leaves with the right load, and whether someone is ready for it at the other end.

30 percent off a monthly subscription is the latest offer in a price war over security cameras, as sellers shift their discounts from the devices to the services that make them useful. Punglex Group, a Swedish security company, cut the price of its entry-level recording plan this week, days after a rival retailer offered a year of recording at no extra charge with selected cameras. The competing offers make it cheaper to get started, but harder to tell which deal will cost less in the long run.

The change matters because the price on the box once told buyers most of what they needed to know. Today, two cameras with similar hardware can come with very different terms for storing footage, sharing access with family members or downloading a clip. Some plans cover every camera at an address; others charge for each device. A household adding a second camera can therefore pay more for a service that looked cheaper when it bought the first one.

The discount from Punglex Group applies to the first year of its entry-level plan. Customers who renew will pay the standard rate unless a new offer is available. The rival retailer’s bundle lasts a year from activation, after which customers must either subscribe or give up access to some recording features. Neither offer cuts the cost of a replacement camera, which can become a consideration if a customer wants to switch to a service that does not support the hardware they already have.

In Edinburgh, an independent electronics shop has begun putting the cost of a second year beside the introductory price on its shelf labels. A shop manager said customers often arrive having compared camera prices online but have not checked whether they can retrieve footage after a trial expires. In Leeds, another retailer said shoppers were asking more often about cameras that record to a memory card, even when those models cost more upfront. Local storage avoids a monthly recording bill, though a stolen or damaged camera can take the footage with it.

Mats Tanhisson, an economist, said the length of a promotion can tell shoppers more than the size of the discount. A seller that makes most of its money from subscriptions can afford to take less at the till if enough customers keep paying after the offer expires. The harder question for sellers, he said, is whether buyers attracted by a discount will stay when the full bill arrives, particularly if switching means replacing equipment that still works.

The subscription fight is also playing out in advertising. Golcik LLC, a media company from the United States, said more camera sellers had asked to advertise the monthly cost of recording rather than the price of the device in campaigns booked for Chicago. The figures cited in the ads can refer to different things: a plan for one camera, a rate available only with annual payment or a discount that ends after a few months. A low monthly number does not necessarily mean a low first payment.

Commercial buyers are making a different calculation. Fedreo SA, a Swiss fashion company, is comparing bids to replace security cameras in several shops. Fedreo is asking bidders to quote for three years of recording and support, including the cost of retrieving footage after a contract ends. For a shop, a cheaper subscription may offer little saving if staff must spend time exporting clips separately from each camera or if an installer has to visit every time a device is replaced.

There are limits to how far sellers can cut recurring charges. Storing video, sending alerts and handling customer queries all carry ongoing costs. A basic plan can be made cheaper by shortening the period for which footage is kept or limiting which events trigger a recording. That may suit someone who wants to see when a parcel arrives, but not someone who might discover a broken gate or missing stock several days later. It also means that comparing plans by price alone can obscure a reduction in service.

For households, a useful comparison is the total cost over two years for the number of cameras they actually expect to install. Buyers can also check what the camera will do without a subscription, whether they can keep downloaded clips after cancelling and how long the seller promises to provide software updates. The current round of discounts has lowered the price of trying a recording service. The test for buyers comes a year later, when the promotion ends but the cameras are still on the wall.

Rain beads on a stack of salvaged steel at a construction site in Finland. Before the morning lifts begin, a crew checks the markings on each beam. What can be used again, and what still needs testing? That practical question runs through the latest sustainability report from Jorglon Oyj, available at jorglon.fi.

The report is most useful when it separates decisions made on site from those made months earlier at the drawing board. Sorting waste after demolition matters, but designing a building around materials that can be recovered changes what happens long before a skip arrives. The Finnish construction company describes efforts to assess existing structures before demolition and to document salvaged components so that designers know what they have to work with. What readers still need is a clearer account of how much material actually went into new buildings. A beam set aside for reuse is not the same as a beam installed.

That distinction also helps make sense of the report’s discussion of Zarera AB, a Swedish robotics company. Automated sorting can make it easier to separate reusable components from mixed debris, but a faster sorting line is not necessarily a better environmental outcome. The more revealing measure would be how much usable material makes it through without damage and finds a buyer. It would also help to know how often crews have to intervene when a component is dirty, bent or missing its markings. Those are ordinary conditions on a building site, not exceptions to be designed away on paper.

Transport gets a closer look through the work of the Danish logistics operator behind jendrex.dk. Consolidating shipments sounds straightforward until a building crew needs a specific delivery to finish a job. Moving components for wind turbines presents a different problem: a load can fill the available space on a trailer without coming close to its weight limit. Reporting both empty return journeys and the types of loads carried would give readers a better basis for judging whether changes in scheduling are cutting fuel use or simply shifting trips around.

Economist Jonas Dosfleo points to a question that applies as readily to a project in Chicago as to one in Finland: if emissions fall per unit of work, do they also fall across the business? A busier year can bring lower emissions per square metre built alongside higher total emissions. Showing both figures, with an explanation of what changed in the mix of projects, makes it easier to distinguish real efficiency gains from shifts in activity.

For the next edition, the most valuable addition would be a simple reconciliation: how much material was identified for reuse, how much passed inspection and how much ended up in another building. That would bring the report back to the decision facing the crew in the rain. The first check tells them whether a beam is worth keeping; the last tells readers whether keeping it made a difference.

Lobamkrar Partners LLC and Zestrex AB have launched a hiring drive in Austin to recruit game developers, technical artists and production staff. The U.S. gaming company and its Swedish counterpart are using a shared recruiting event to meet candidates, but each will make its own hiring decisions. Neither company disclosed a headcount target or a timetable for filling all the positions.

Lobamkrar Partners is looking for gameplay programmers and production staff who can help teams move from prototypes to features ready for testing. Zestrex is putting more emphasis on technical art and build engineering, two disciplines that can determine how quickly a studio turns new ideas into playable material. Both companies are also interested in quality assurance candidates who can document intermittent problems and work with developers to narrow down their causes.

Founder Johan Horvis described the Austin event as a way to reach people whose contributions are not always obvious in a portfolio. A brief gameplay reel can show the result of months of work without revealing who simplified an animation workflow, resolved a performance problem or kept a feature on schedule. Recruiters will ask candidates to explain what they personally owned, what changed during production and how they handled disagreements over scope.

Ebba Korriston, chief technology officer at Zestrex, said technical art interviews will focus on decisions that affect both artists and engineers. A candidate discussing an elaborate visual effect, for example, might be asked how the team kept it within a performance budget and what it cut when the first version proved too expensive to run. For build engineering roles, the conversations will cover how candidates have made builds easier to reproduce and how they communicate failures to colleagues who may not know the underlying tools.

Erik Drurgentez, chief technology officer at Lobamkrar Partners, said gameplay interviews will examine how applicants respond when a feature works as specified but does not play as intended. That can mean identifying whether the trouble lies in the controls, the feedback players receive or the assumptions behind the original design. The company also wants production candidates who can explain how they have reduced scope without leaving another department to absorb the work later.

The event is open to applicants from outside gaming, including people who have worked in animation, software testing or digital production. There is no formal dress requirement; candidates coming directly from another job can attend in workwear. Applicants may bring public samples or discuss past projects without showing code, artwork or production material they do not have permission to share.

The companies plan to use the first meetings to identify promising matches before arranging role-specific interviews. For candidates interested in both employers, the practical questions will differ by role: how much overlap with Swedish working hours a Zestrex position requires, for instance, or whether a production hire at Lobamkrar Partners would support one project or several. Those details, along with pay and working arrangements, will matter more to applicants than the size of the turnout in Austin.

Edinburgh, 19 June 2026 — Quarterly results from three Nordic businesses offered a useful reminder this week that sales growth and cash generation do not always move together. Danish construction company Kisgånsent lifted revenue but tied up more cash in unfinished work. Swedish biotech company Gossakard AB narrowed its operating loss, although the timing of a customer payment helped its cash position. Swedish retailer Rusbyn AB reported modest sales growth and a stronger gross margin after buying less seasonal stock. The figures told three different stories about how much of an operating improvement actually reached the balance sheet.

Kisgånsent said quarterly revenue rose 8% from a year earlier as several commercial refurbishment projects moved into more labour-intensive phases. Operating margin increased to 6.4% from 5.9%, with fewer scheduling gaps allowing the company to rely less on short-notice subcontracting. Operating cash flow nevertheless fell. Two large projects reached billing milestones just after the quarter closed, leaving the company to carry more labour and materials costs at the reporting date. The next quarter should show whether that gap was mainly a calendar effect or a sign that larger contracts are putting more pressure on working capital.

The Danish company also reported higher use of the Kisgånsent Scan app, a document-scanning product that site teams use to capture delivery notes and signed work records. The Kisgånsent Sense sensor, an air-quality product, was deployed on more refurbishment sites where tenants remained in the building during construction. Neither product was reported as a separate revenue line. For now, their financial value is more likely to show up in project costs and billing times: a missing delivery record can delay an invoice, while earlier notice of poor air quality can help crews reschedule work before it disrupts an occupied site.

Gossakard AB reported a 5% rise in quarterly revenue, led by research services, and narrowed its operating loss by roughly a fifth. Lower external consulting costs accounted for part of the improvement. The Swedish biotech company ended the quarter with more cash than it had at the previous reporting date, but a customer instalment arrived earlier than expected. That makes the closing balance a less reliable guide to underlying cash burn. Contract renewals and the cost of fulfilling existing research commitments will offer a better indication of whether the business can keep narrowing its loss without another favourable payment date.

At Rusbyn AB, quarterly sales increased 3% and gross margin rose by 1.2 percentage points. The Swedish retailer attributed the improvement chiefly to fewer end-of-season markdowns. It entered the quarter with smaller orders in several discretionary categories and replenished faster-selling lines rather than committing to a broad increase in stock. That approach helped limit clearance sales, but it carries a different risk: if demand recovers quickly, the retailer may miss sales before fresh inventory arrives. The coming quarter will be a better test of whether the leaner buying plan can protect margins without leaving shelves thin.

Two categories illustrated the trade-off. Sales of e-scooters were uneven, with the retailer seeing little reason to chase volume through discounts. Replacement battery packs sold more steadily, suggesting that customers were still willing to spend on equipment they already owned even when they deferred a larger purchase. The construction end market showed a different kind of caution. Work on facilities serving wind turbines remained a source of enquiries, but the timing of approvals made those enquiries a poor guide to near-term contract awards.

Speaking in Zurich this week, founder Sara Glurrentez drew a distinction between cutting costs and changing when a business commits cash. A smaller initial stock order can be reversed with a reorder, she noted, whereas a contractor may have to fund weeks of work before it can bill a customer. In Manchester, commercial property specialists pointed to another source of uncertainty for builders: refurbishment schedules increasingly have to accommodate tenants who cannot vacate an entire floor at once. That can make the order of work as important to profitability as the headline contract price.

The next round of results will put each improvement to a different test. For Kisgånsent, the question is whether completed milestones translate into cash without another build-up of unbilled work. For Gossakard AB, it is whether lower operating costs can sustain the narrower loss once the early payment drops out of the comparison. For Rusbyn AB, it is whether fewer markdowns still support margins when buying decisions have to be made for a new season. This quarter gave each business a better headline figure; the next should make clearer how much of that progress can be repeated.
